backups.fa: Forest Farr, Art Winder, Laurence Byington (1930)
gear: glacier axe and crampons (or microspikes if the glacier has consolidated to hard ice late season)
hazards: loose/choss rock in the entry gully and lower pitches — test every hold

backups.overview: The East Face is Chimney Rock's most commonly climbed and documented line to the true Main/Central Summit (7,727 ft) — the same summit reached by the peak's 1930 first ascent. From a high camp near the toe of the Chimney Glacier, parties rope up and cross the glacier and its bergschrund/moat to reach three pitches of low-fifth-class (5.3) rock: a lichen-covered chimney, an exposed 4th-class traverse, and a final chimney that tops out just below the summit cairn. It's a long, remote objective — most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip, with roughly 19 miles and 6,000 ft of elevation gain/loss round trip from the Pete Lake Trailhead.
backups.beta: From high camp, ascend moraine to the Chimney Glacier, cross the bergschrund via snow/ice blocks, then scramble exposed 4th-class ledges to the Main Notch between the South and Main peaks. From the notch, a 3rd/4th-class 'reddish ramp' and further scrambling lead to a broad ledge below the summit tower, where climbers rack up for 3 roped pitches to the top. Rock is generally sound but has loose ('choss') sections; many parties note the bergschrund/moat crossing is often the technical crux of the day, not the rock pitches.
backups.turnaround: Set a hard turnaround time before starting the technical pitches — the glacier crossing and bergschrund become more hazardous as the day warms and snow bridges soften, and afternoon thunderstorms are common in the Cascades in summer.
backups.rappels: Single ~165 ft rope; two or three rappels from the summit down to the broad ledge (Key Ledge), then 2 rappels near the bergschrund plus downclimbing between them
backups.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass to park at most trailheads.
backups.descent: Rappel the East Face back to the glacier, then reverse the approach.

backups.detailed_rack: Light-to-moderate alpine trad rack: stoppers/nuts, cams up to ~3 inches, plenty of slings, and spare webbing/cord for weathered rappel anchors.
pro_tips: Cross the Chimney Glacier in early morning while still firm/frozen for safer, faster travel
Plan for a 3-day trip; without an efficient early start many parties don't reach the base of the technical climbing until late in the day
Assess crevasse/moat conditions from recent trip reports before committing — they change significantly through the season
The entry gully in the lower rock band is often wet and holds loose blocks — test each hold before committing.
watch_out: test all holds — the face still holds loose blocks despite decades of cleaning
the moat/bergschrund crossing varies hugely by year and season — some parties find an easy ice ramp, others find it nearly impassable
cross the glacier early before the surface softens
backups.pro_needs: A moderate trad rack (stoppers plus cams roughly 0.5–1 inch) covers the crux chimney and ledge systems; bring extra slings for tat at rappel anchors.
backups.best_season: Mid-July through September, after the Chimney Glacier's bergschrund/crevasses consolidate
backups.approach: From the Pete Lake Trailhead off FR 4616 (elev. ~2,850 ft), follow the Pete Lake Trail #1323 west and north through open, nearly-flat forest along Cooper River/Lemah Meadow terrain — easy tread and wildflower meadows for about 4 miles to the south shore of Pete Lake, a popular first camp and reliable water source. Continue past the lake roughly 2 more miles to the Pacific Crest Trail junction near Escondido Ridge and turn north onto the PCT. After about a mile of PCT travel, watch for a wide avalanche path with heavy blowdown crossing the trail near the confluence of Chimney Creek — this is the turnoff for the climb. Leave the PCT and work climber's-right across the avalanche debris to pick up a boot/climber's path on the true-right side of Chimney Creek (it starts roughly 20 yards inside the timber and is marked intermittently with orange flagging and cairns). The path fords back to creek-left after about 200 yards, crosses three brushy ravines, and pushes through alder and vine maple before breaking into open moraine and a hanging basin — cairns mark the line through this stretch, which is the main route-finding crux of the approach. A rock buttress called Sunrise Knob (~4,650 ft), overlooking Chimney Creek's waterfalls, marks the top of the brush; most parties reach it in 4-5 hours from the trailhead. From Sunrise Knob, climb the moraine crest to roughly 5,400 ft and a boulder-strewn basin at the toe of the Chimney Glacier — a large boulder near the creek has 3+ established bivy sites and is the standard high camp (most parties treat this as a 2-3 day trip). Reliable water is at Pete Lake and the low Chimney Creek crossings; above the moraine plan on melting snow or glacier water. Hazards: the avalanche-path crossing (blowdown, lingering snow/avalanche debris into early summer), loose/brushy ravine crossings, and standard glacier travel hazards (crevasses, moats) gaining and crossing the Chimney Glacier to the base of the route.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line rather than continuing over the summit block. From the summit, rappel the three summit pitches back to the broad ledge below the tower (two or three rappels on a single rope), then traverse back through the notch/gully between the main and south summits (a short reversal of the ascent gully, Class 3-4 downclimbing over loose debris or snow/ice depending on season). Where the rock steepens near the base of the face, on the wet, lower-angle slabs just above the glacier, most parties make two rappels over these fourth-class steps using a single rope (a 50-60m/165ft rope is enough for each); anchors here are natural — slung horns and blocks rather than bolts — so carry cord/webbing to back up or replace old tat, especially early in the season. Below the raps, a final short third-class downclimb regains the bergschrund/moat crossing back onto the Chimney Glacier, then reverse the moraine and climber's path to Sunrise Knob and the Pete Lake Trail. Note: some parties, especially those who climbed a more direct line up the face, instead reverse the entire face with a longer string of rappels — trip reports for the harder Direct East Face variant describe as many as five to six rappels straight down the glacier-facing slabs with good anchors reported the whole way down — but the descent via the saddle/gully is the more commonly reported line for the standard East Face route. Watch for loose rock/rockfall in the gully, wet slick rock on the fourth-class rappel steps, and crevasse/moat hazard back on the glacier.
backups.bail: Retreat down the same line: downclimb or rappel the pitches and ledges back to the Main Notch, then reverse the glacier/moraine descent; the rope carried for summit rappels is sufficient to bail from any point on the tower.

July.reason: Early July still has snow-covered slopes and a filled-in schrund; by late July the glacier firms and access to the rock is straightforward.

June.reason: Heavy snow on the Chimney Creek climbers' path and glacier, and avalanche runout from the steep basin above the PCT turnoff.

August.reason: Dry rock on the chimney pitches; the icefall and bergschrund open up, so expect hard 45-degree ice or a moat crossing on collapsed blocks.

October.reason: New snow on loose entry-gully ledges, bare icy glacier, and the Pete Lake trailhead road nears its seasonal end.

September.reason: The glacier goes to bare ice, the moat at the base of the face can become hard to enter, and days shorten on a 3-day trip.

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake trail and the PCT, then the Chimney Creek climbers' path to the moraine basin
approach_variants.notes: Start at the Pete Lake trailhead off Cooper Lake Road, FR 46 then FR 4616. Trailhead elevations are given from about 2,790 to 2,900 ft, so do not treat any one figure as exact. A Northwest Forest Pass is required and this is Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Bikes are allowed on roughly the first two and a half miles of trail and no further. Walk the Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River, about four flat forested miles to Pete Lake, then on past the lake staying left at the forks to meet the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT roughly a mile to a mile and a half. The turn-off is a landmark, not a mileage, and parties consistently describe it the same way: the trail crosses an old avalanche swathe at about 3,360 ft and switchbacks sharply. Stop at that hairpin and look west across the valley. Twin waterfalls come down out of a hanging basin — that meltwater is coming off the Chimney Glacier and that basin is where you are going. To the right of the falls are two rounded rock outcrops and further right a cliff band; the climbers' path goes up the forest between the rounded outcrops and the cliff band. One party puts its start at an obvious logjam giving creek access, only about twenty yards inside the forest rather than the two hundred sometimes given. Orange flagging appears in places and should not be relied on. One known wrong turn on that path: it climbs north-west and runs up to a rocky gully. Do not go up the rocky gully. The line continues left through vine maple and bracken fern, where the tread is buried under a season's growth. The path crosses three ravines, the second being the awkward one, and reaches bivy ground below the moraine. A rock buttress above the waterfalls is known as Sunrise Knob at roughly 4,650 to 4,700 ft; another party camped in a meadow at about 4,800 ft. Times from the car to that camp are reported anywhere from four and a half to over six hours, and planning three days is a common recommendation for what many parties attempt in two.
approach_variants.season: Early summer is better than late here. As the season runs on the glacier opens up and the moat at the foot of the rock becomes the thing that turns parties around
hazards: The moat and bergschrund at the base of the east face, which can be impassable late season
Crevasses on the Chimney Glacier and an active icefall between the lower and upper sections
Very serious route-finding — a well-known serious fall on this peak happened off route
Loose rock throughout the summit ledges and gullies
Vine maple and bracken burying the climbers' path, and flagging that may lead nowhere
Mosquitoes heavy down at lake level
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the bivy the thing to identify is the U-Gap, the notch that almost every party climbing this peak passes through. Chimney Rock is the second peak to the right of the U-Gap. Fix that relationship from camp, in daylight, before you are on the glacier. Getting onto the upper glacier is a three-way choice and it is always the same three: a rock or snow gully in the cliff band just left of the icefall (the usual, described as grungy and wet), a snow finger far to the left, or the icefall climbed directly if you have screws and the conditions for it. The moat is the arrival, and whether you can get from snow onto rock at all is the crux of the day rather than a formality. Parties describe reaching the bergschrund at the foot of the face and finding it large, then getting across only because fallen ice blocks had tumbled in and built a ramp and platform to step off. If there is no such ramp there may be no way onto the rock, and that is a condition of the season, not a route-finding failure. Above the U-Gap the traverse across the South Peak toward the Main Peak is a sequence of ledges that one party fairly called improbable — the first of them begins about fifteen vertical feet below the U-Gap on its east side, so a search at gap level finds nothing. Negative marker worth carrying: the blind chimney on the way to the broad ledge under the summit tower was found by one party to be a very loose, dangerous, grungy gully. They backed out of it and instead downclimbed about fifty feet from the Main Notch and picked up an obvious reddish third-to-fourth-class ramp leading to the small notch they wanted. If you are grovelling in rotten grunge you are probably in the feature they abandoned. A final sanity check on how rarely this is done: the summit register suggests roughly one party a year. Do not expect a boot track or fresh tat to confirm anything for you.

climbing_route.label: Lower Chimney Glacier to the upper glacier
climbing_route.notes: Rope up at the toe and climb the lower glacier. Three ways have been used to break through the cliff band onto the upper glacier; the common one is the rock and snow gully just left of the icefall. Crevasses and the icefall are the hazards, and the gully can be running with meltwater later in the day — an early start pays here twice over.

climbing_route.label: Upper glacier and the moat
climbing_route.notes: Cross the upper glacier to the foot of the gully that climbs to the U-Gap. A moat routinely forms where the ice pulls away from the rock and it is the crux of getting on the route: in some conditions collapsed ice blocks have bridged it into a usable ramp and platform, in others it needs a belayed step across or a detour. Assess this from a distance on the way in, because the alternative is a long traverse looking for a way on.

climbing_route.label: U-Gap, the South Peak ledges and the Main Notch to the Key Ledge
climbing_route.notes: From the moat, climb the loose gully to the U-Gap, then leave it on its east side, starting about fifteen feet below the gap, and follow the exposed ledges that wrap around the South Peak to the Main Notch between the South and Main summits. Most of it is third-class scrambling with short fourth-class steps, often on wet rock, and running belays are the usual compromise. From the Main Notch drop roughly fifty feet and take a reddish third-to-fourth-class ramp up to the broad ledge beneath the summit tower, the Key Ledge, which has a few bivy spots but no dependable water.

climbing_route.label: Summit pitches
climbing_route.notes: Three pitches of class 4 and low fifth class slabs finish the climb, roughly two and a half hours from the ledge, with the hardest moves around 5.4 to 5.6 — Grade II overall. The first pitch takes low-fifth ground on generally sound rock and protects adequately with slings, stoppers and small cams up to about three quarters of an inch. Above it a short traverse crosses a small heathered ledge onto a very exposed fourth-class face. The last pitch is a clean low-fifth chimney that tops out a few feet from the summit cairn. Rock shoes are worth carrying for this section.

climbing_route.label: Rappel descent
climbing_route.notes: Rappel the summit pitches back to the Key Ledge (two or three rappels), reverse the ledges and the Main Notch mostly by downclimbing, then make two short rappels over the wet fourth-class steps near the base of the rock before a last third-class downclimb to the moat. A single 165 ft rope has been sufficient. Back the anchors up rather than trusting old tat, keep the ropes clear of the loose ledges, and leave enough daylight — the moat crossing back onto the glacier is the last problem of the day, not the first.

bivy.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
bivy.notes: This is Chimney Rock's real base, and it is the reason parties take the Cle Elum side rather than the Middle Fork. From Pete Lake continue to the PCT, turn north, and at the second switchback where the trail starts up toward Waptus Pass leave it westward through open forest, dropping slightly to the North Fork of Lemah Creek at around 3,380 ft. Cross on a log — the crossing is the crux of the approach in high water — and find the boot path on the far side, marked by a large cairn with faded flagging for the first couple of hundred feet. It climbs steeply, roughly 1,400 ft, into the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier. Aim for the huge boulder near the creek in the middle of the basin. Round trip from the car is on the order of thirty miles for the peak, so this is a two- or three-night trip for most parties, and it puts the East Face and East Face Direct within a reasonable summit day. The same basin serves the standard West Face and South Summit line by way of the glacier and the notch. Best from mid-July to mid-September: earlier and the glacier crossing is straightforward but the approach is a snow slog, later and the ice is bare and crevassed. Expect no company. The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.
bivy.water: Meltwater creek running through the basin, dependable while the glacier is melting; late in a dry September it can shrink and want a walk uphill
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.
bivy.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that

bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.
bivy.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

backups.overview: Mount Crowder (7,082 ft) is a remote outlying summit on the eastern crest of the Picket Range, North Cascades National Park, sitting near the divide between the Goodell Creek and Picket Creek (Baker River) drainages roughly 1.6 mi southwest of Mount Fury and just south of its parent peak, Phantom Peak. It has 1,042 ft of prominence and 1.53 mi of isolation. First climbed in 1962 by Cal Magnusson, Jack Ardussi, Don Mech, and Don Schmechel when it was still known informally as 'Old Brownie,' the peak was officially renamed in 1970 by the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to honor Dr. Dwight F. Crowder (1929-1970), a USGS geologist, mountaineer, and North Cascades conservationist credited with several first ascents in the range, including South Spectacle Butte and Sitkum Spire. Crowder sits deep in the trailless heart of the Pickets and is almost never climbed as a standalone objective — nearly all recorded ascents are one summit within a multi-day Picket Range ridge enchainment.
backups.beta: Once through the approach and the infamous 'Crowder Bypass,' the SW Flank itself is a moderate 3rd/4th-class scramble on open slopes and ledges to the summit — no technical rock climbing required. Parties doing a standalone ascent typically descend the way they came; parties continuing a larger Pickets traverse instead descend the far more serious NE Ridge toward Pickell Pass.
backups.turnaround: Given the multi-day, off-trail approach and the lack of an easy retreat off the NE side, set a firm daily turnaround time that gets you back to camp/water before dark — there is no quick descent if you're caught out on Crowder's upper flanks.
backups.rappels: 0 on the standard descent - reversing the SW Flank is a walk-off on 2nd/3rd-class scree and heather. Carry the rope anyway: the NE Ridge line toward Pickell Pass typically needs a short rappel past a cliff band and a chasm, which is what this route's 30 m rope and anchor slings are for.
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: This is one of the most remote corners of North Cascades National Park; expect no reliable cell coverage for the majority of the approach and climb — carry a satellite communicator or PLB.
backups.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

backups.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the SW Flank scramble itself. An ice axe (and often traction) is standard for the steep snow sections of the Crowder Bypass and approach ridge. Parties planning the alternative NE Ridge descent (as part of a larger traverse) commonly carry a light rope and a small rack/slings for the short 4th/5th-class downclimbing and occasional rappel.
what_to_bring: a few slings and small cams/nuts for rappel anchors
bear canister/food storage per current NPS regulations
pro_tips: Climb the SW Flank early in the day while any residual snow/scree is firm; it becomes loose and tedious later in the day.
Carry a light rope (30m) even on the standard route — parties have used it for a short rappel or belayed step on both the SW Flank and especially the NE side.
Early-to-mid August (as in the best-documented 2012 ascent) offers the most reliable snow-free conditions; July can still have lingering snow in approach gullies.
watch_out: The NE Ridge descent toward Pickell Pass looks like a reasonable alternate way down but hides a several-hundred-foot chasm and a cliff band that has forced parties to rappel — don't commit to it without a rope and rappel gear.
Big Beaver Creek must be forded on the northern approach; it can be difficult or dangerous to cross during snowmelt.
This is multi-day, no-cell-coverage terrain — carry a satellite communicator and file a detailed itinerary.
backups.pro_needs: Minimal rock gear — a few slings and small cams/nuts are enough for the occasional short rappel anchor or belayed step; this is a scrambling route, not a pitched rock climb.
backups.approach: Mount Crowder has no trailhead and no maintained trail — every ascent is layered onto a multi-day, off-trail traverse through the heart of the Picket Range, and Crowder is almost never climbed as a standalone objective. Parties reach it via one of two corridors. From the south: the Goodell Creek climbers' path (turn off WA-20 opposite Newhalem into Goodell Creek Campground; the boot path starts behind a large boulder at the campground) climbs steeply and brushily through slide alder and old-growth timber, gaining roughly 2,500 ft in about a mile to reach the basins below McMillan Spire/Inspiration Peak in the Southern Pickets; from there it's a rugged, unmarked cross-country traverse north over intervening cols (Crescent Creek Basin, the shoulder east of Mount Terror, and bypasses around the McMillan Cirque "Barrier") toward the range's central saddle area. From the north/east: the Big Beaver Trail out of the Ross Dam trailhead on Ross Lake (often shortened with the Ross Lake Resort water taxi to Big Beaver/Beaver Pass Camp), leaving trail to climb Access Creek — staying on its north-flank benches through semi-open forest to about 3,700 ft, where brush thickens and a faint, cairned climbers' path crosses to the south bank and continues to the open basin at the creek's headwaters (reliable water, good camping). From either entry, Crowder itself is gained by traversing the connecting ridge past Pioneer Peak and Phantom Peak to Wild Pass, a heather-and-talus notch overlooking the small tarn of Wild Lake just below; from the pass, cross open slopes to the col between Phantom Peak and Crowder, then climb the broad SW Flank — tersely put, "climb SW from the col" — up easy 2nd/3rd-class scree, heather ramps, and low-angle rock to the summit. There is no reliable water above Wild Lake, and the connecting terrain between passes is exposed talus and heather with genuine routefinding difficulty in poor visibility; expect several full days of off-trail travel carrying multi-day loads to even reach Wild Pass.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the SW Flank exactly as climbed: down the easy 2nd/3rd-class scree and heather ramps to the Phantom–Crowder col, then back over to Wild Pass above Wild Lake. This is a walk-off/downclimb on the standard route — no rappels are required. Do not be tempted to shortcut east off the NE Ridge toward Pickell Pass: a first-hand account found this alternative deceptively difficult — in practice descending it means weaving a convoluted line of grassy 3rd-class ledges broken by short, exposed 4th-class and even a couple of 5th-class downclimbing moves, past a major chasm/fault splitting the lower ridge, with an unprotectable vertical drop near the base that forced one climber in that party to rig an improvised rappel off natural gear (there is no fixed hardware anywhere on this peak) rather than downclimb it. On the standard SW Flank descent, plan on 0 rappels; a rope is not needed for the reversal, just careful 3rd-class scrambling technique and, ideally, a GPS track of your ascent line given the routefinding-heavy terrain.
backups.bail: The SW Flank is the only realistic bail-out line; once committed to the NE Ridge toward Pickell Pass, retreat is difficult due to the chasm and cliff band, so treat that side as effectively one-way.

climate.fall: Weather deteriorates and snow returns by roughly early October, matching the point at which NPS backcountry camping fees stop being charged for the season.
climate.spring: Approach passes typically remain heavily snow-covered into June/July, easing brush travel but adding steep-snow and avalanche exposure.
climate.summer: July and the first weeks of August are the most reliably dry and stable; by mid-to-late August nearby glaciers and moats open up and can complicate approach terrain, though the SW Flank itself is non-glaciated.
climate.winter: Effectively inaccessible for climbing; deep snowpack and avalanche hazard affect all approaches.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast alpine climate typical of the North Cascades crest — heavy winter snowpack, a wet, slow-to-clear spring, and a comparatively drier but still unsettled summer. An unnamed glacier occupies Crowder's north cirque.

bySeason.fall: Early snow and rime can arrive by late September, adding difficulty to the already-loose SW Flank and the NE Ridge's exposed sections.
bySeason.spring: Approach creek fords (Big Beaver, Access Creek) run high and cold with snowmelt; upper gullies typically still hold snow.
bySeason.summer: July through September is the historically favorable window for a snow-free SW Flank; the best-documented ascent was made August 12.
bySeason.winter: Deep snowpack and avalanche exposure make the peak essentially inaccessible.

backups.name: Nohokomeen Glacier and Headwall
gear: Ice axe plus a second technical tool
hazards: Crevasse fall on the Nohokomeen Glacier, which is heavily crevassed below its midpoint.
Bergschrund crossing on a single snow bridge, worsening with warmth and season.
Avalanche and wet-slide hazard on a 700-800 ft face of 50-60 degree snow, particularly once the sun is on it.
Cornice failure on the north-facing summit ridge.
A long unroped fall is the consequence of a slip anywhere on the headwall - self-arrest on 55-60 degree snow is unreliable.
Extreme remoteness: 11 miles from the road, no cell coverage, and a multi-day evacuation for any injury.
backups.overview: The classic north-side snow route on Jack Mountain and by far the best documented line on the peak: the East Bank Trail to May Creek, a steep bushwhack to the Nohokomeen Glacier, then roughly 2,100 ft of crevassed glacier and a 700-800 ft headwall of sustained 50-60 degree snow to a corniced summit ridge. The round trip is rated at 30 miles and 10,000 ft of gain and graded an intermediate alpine climb.
backups.beta: This is an early-season snow climb, done when the north cirque is still filled in. From the East Bank Trailhead follow the East Bank Trail roughly 8 miles to the May Creek camp, then leave the trail and climb about 3 miles of steep, bushy, cliff-banded forest — cliff bands start around 3,200 ft and are passed on game trails — to reach snowline near 4,800-5,000 ft and a camp either on the flats around 5,200 ft below the glacier or higher on the glacier itself around 7,400 ft. The Nohokomeen Glacier runs from about 6,100 ft to 8,200 ft, is over 340 acres, and is heavily crevassed after the midpoint of its descent, so rope up. Above the glacier the headwall is the crux: it is variously described as 700 vertical feet of snow at slopes up to 60 degrees, and as a sustained 50-55 degrees for about 800 feet with steeper steps. Most parties simul-climb it, taking turns kicking steps, with a rope over the shoulder for the bergschrund; winter parties have pitched it out with pickets, cams, nuts and screws through a mixed cliff band. The bergschrund is the main obstacle and normally goes on a single bridge on the left side. Above, exit onto the ridge and finish along a narrow, corniced summit ridge with rocky drops — the last few hundred feet are the most exposed of the route.
backups.turnaround: This is a snow climb, so turn on snow, not on a clock. Go down if the headwall has softened to the point that steps collapse or an axe shaft no longer holds, if the bergschrund bridge is degrading and you doubt you can recross it, if cornices on the summit ridge are unsupported or the ridge is loaded with fresh wind slab, or if cloud closes in and you cannot see the line back through the glacier. Be off the headwall before the sun has been on it long — every party that reports a clean ascent was down off the face by mid-morning to noon.
backups.rappels: No fixed rappels and no established rappel line. The standard descent is downclimbing/simul-downclimbing the ascent route; parties that want protection lower off buried pickets on the steepest ~100 m of the headwall. A 60 m rope is the norm.
backups.comms: No cell service at the East Bank Trailhead, on the East Bank Trail, or anywhere in the Nohokomeen cirque. A satellite messenger or PLB is essential; note that the deep north-facing cirque has poor sky view, so send messages from the open glacier or from the ridge. Ross Lake Resort's boat traffic is the only regular human presence anywhere nearby. Nearest staffed contact: North Cascades Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount, 360-854-7245.
backups.descent: Downclimb the ascent line: reverse the headwall (simul-downclimbing or lowering off buried pickets), recross the bergschrund, then descend the glacier and the bushwhack to camp.

From the lot the trail drops briefly to the bridge over Ruby Creek, so there is no further driving once you are here. If you come before the highway opens for the season, the gate is back at milepost 134, and parties have biked the roughly four miles in to the trailhead from there and continued on foot or ski.

timing.recommendedStart: From a glacier camp, leave between 4:00 and 4:30 a.m. so the headwall is climbed on a firm overnight refreeze and you are off the face by mid-morning. From a low camp at ~5,200 ft, a 6:30 a.m. departure has produced an 18-hour day - start earlier.

backups.detailed_rack: A snow rack, not a rock rack. Carry a 60 m rope per rope team, harnesses, a full crevasse-rescue kit (prusiks, pulley, three or four locking carabiners), and three to four snow pickets — pickets are the workhorse here, used for the bergschrund, for running belays on the headwall and for lowering on the descent. Two ice screws are worth carrying for the years when the headwall turns out to be ice rather than neve. Most parties climb with one axe plus one technical tool each; on the winter ascent through the cliff band, teams carried one technical and one straight-shafted tool per climber plus cams, nuts, hexes and screws. Add snowshoes or skis for the approach and glacier, which most parties use.
what_to_bring: Tent, sleeping bag and stove for 2-3 nights
Shell and insulating layers - the north cirque is cold and shaded
Headlamp and spare batteries (long pre-dawn starts and a real chance of finishing in the dark)
GPS with the bushwhack line recorded on the way up - navigating the timber at night is the crux of many trips
Sunglasses and full sun protection for the glacier
2-3 L water capacity and a stove to melt snow at a glacier camp
Gaiters and gear you do not mind soaking on the bushwhack
Skis or a splitboard if you want the descent as a bonus - the glacier has been skied
pro_tips: Go in a cold window in May. Every report says the same thing: earlier is better because the bergschrund opens fast, and waiting until June can shut the route down.
Record a GPS track on the way UP through the bushwhack. Multiple parties have relied on it to find their way back through the cliff bands after dark.
A high camp on the glacier around 7,400 ft turns a brutal 18-hour summit day into a comfortable morning, at the cost of hauling a heavier pack up the bushwhack.
Cross the bergschrund early. The single bridge on the left side that parties report using is a morning feature; by afternoon it is markedly worse.
Consider the Ross Lake Resort water taxi. It removes most of the 8-mile trail approach and is a legitimate, established way in.
Kick good steps on the way up - you will be downclimbing them, and having them is what makes the descent reasonable.
Do not confuse this with the 'Northeast Glacier' route, which is a different and far less documented line on the other side of the north ridge.
watch_out: The bergschrund is the crux and it degrades through the day and through the season; know how you will recross it before you climb above it.
The summit ridge is narrow and corniced with rocky drops - it has caught out otherwise competent parties.
Snow structure on the headwall has repeatedly been reported as suspect: thin ice crusts 2 and 4 inches down over dense powder, or deep sugary snow high on the face.
The 3-mile bushwhack from May Creek is steep, cliff-banded and easy to lose in the dark; it is the reason parties finish at midnight.
Below-average snow years expose rock on the headwall and turn a pure snow climb into a mixed one.
SR 20's winter gate at MP 134 adds about 4 miles each way of biking or skiing before the highway opens.
backups.pro_needs: Pickets for snow, screws as a backup for ice, and a rock anchor or two only if the headwall's cliff band is melted out and you must climb mixed ground. In good May conditions most parties place almost nothing and simul-climb the headwall, so protection is more about having a retreat plan than about protecting the leader.
backups.best_season: A cold window in May is the consensus best time: long days, a stable and still-continuous snowpack, and a bergschrund that has not yet opened. Waiting until June is problematic because the schrund opens rapidly. Early May trips have found powder rather than ice on the headwall. Winter ascents have been made (January and early May are both documented) but require biking or skiing in from the SR 20 closure gate and full avalanche, cornice and crevasse competence. This route is emphatically not a late-summer objective.
backups.approach: From SR 20 milepost 138, park at the East Bank Trailhead (~1,800 ft) and descend briefly to the bridge over Ruby Creek. Follow the East Bank Trail — mostly flat and fast — roughly 8 miles north along Ross Lake to the May Creek camp. (Ross Lake Resort's water taxi will drop parties on the eastern shore and is a legitimate way to skip most of the trail; check current rates and schedule directly with the resort.) At May Creek leave the trail and climb steeply west-to-northwest, loosely ascending between the creeks on the west side of Jack Mountain. Cliff bands begin around 3,200 ft and are threaded on boot and game trails; snow generally appears around 4,800-5,000 ft. About 3 miles of this off-trail work reaches a flat camp just over 5,200 ft below the glacier toe. Strong parties push a second camp onto the upper glacier around 7,400 ft, which shortens summit day considerably. Before the highway opens, parties have biked about 4 miles from the MP 134 gate to the trailhead and continued on foot or ski.
backups.descent_text: There is no rappel line — the standard descent is to downclimb what you climbed, ideally in your own steps. Reverse the corniced summit ridge carefully, then face-in downclimb the headwall; parties that are not comfortable simul-downclimbing 50-60 degree snow lower each other off buried pickets on the steepest 100 m or so. Recross the bergschrund at the same bridge you used on the way up, and be aware that it will be softer and less trustworthy than it was in the morning. Descend the glacier roped, aiming to be off the snow before it crusts up or, in spring, before afternoon warming makes the lower slopes unstable. From the glacier toe, retrace the bushwhack down through the cliff bands to camp — this is genuinely hard to navigate in the dark and several parties have relied on GPS to find their line back through the timber. Reported summit-to-camp times run from about 2.5 hours (fast, in good steps) to considerably longer. From camp it is the 3-mile descent to May Creek and 8 miles of flat trail back to the car.
backups.bail: From the headwall, downclimbing is the bail — it is the same as the descent, so the decision is simply whether to keep going up. Carry enough pickets to lower off if someone cannot downclimb. Below the bergschrund, retreat is a straightforward glacier descent to camp. The real commitment is the approach: once you are camped above May Creek you are 11 miles from the road with 3 of those being a steep bushwhack, so a bail is a long day but never technical. Bad weather in the cirque, a bergschrund that has opened past crossing, or snow that has warmed into instability are the three normal reasons to go down.

pitch_detail.notes: From the toe of the Nohokomeen Glacier around 6,100 ft to the upper glacier bench around 8,200 ft (elevation range per the USGS glacier record). Heavily crevassed below the midpoint - travel roped and navigate around the icefall sections. Snowshoes or skis are useful low down.

The main obstacle. Parties report a single usable bridge on the left side of the face, directly below the summit; in lean years a traverse right across melted rock bands is needed to gain the headwall. This is the feature that closes the route by June.
Sustained snow climbing, normally simul-climbed with climbers alternating the lead and kicking steps. Pickets for running belays if conditions are poor.

The face steepens near the top - slopes up to 60 degrees are reported. Snow quality is the variable: parties have found anything from perfect neve to deep sugary snow over thin crusts. In lean years a rock cliff band here forces a mixed pitch.
Exit the headwall onto a narrow, corniced ridge with rocky drops and traverse to the true summit. Short, but the most exposed part of the route; keep well back from the cornice line.

backups.itinerary: Three days is the normal plan and is what most parties use; strong teams do it in two. Day 1: trailhead to May Creek (8 miles of easy trail, roughly 3-3.5 hours), then 3 miles of steep bushwhack to a camp at ~5,200 ft below the glacier, or push on to a glacier camp near 7,400 ft (a 6 a.m. start has reached a 7,400 ft glacier camp by 5 p.m.). Day 2: leave camp around 4-4:30 a.m., cross the glacier, climb the headwall and the summit ridge (summit typically 7:45-8:45 a.m. from a high camp, or roughly 4-5 hours from a 5,200 ft camp), then downclimb and return. Day 3: descend the bushwhack and hike out the East Bank Trail. One documented two-day trip covered camp-to-summit-and-back in an 18-hour push from the low camp.

access.fees: No entrance fee and no parking fee at the East Bank Trailhead. Backcountry permits are free.
access.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required for any overnight stay at a designated camp on the East Bank Trail, including May Creek; permits are limited and are obtained at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center or Hozomeen. Camping higher up, once you are in the Pasayten Wilderness, is covered by a free self-issued Forest Service wilderness permit.
access.closures: SR 20 winter closure between MP 134 and MP 171. May Creek has a difficult stock crossing, and various East Bank Trail bridges have been out in recent years; Hozomeen Lake (well north of this route) is closed April 1 - May 31 for loon nesting. Check current trail status with the Wilderness Information Center.
access.landManager: Split management: the East Bank Trailhead and the East Bank Trail are in Ross Lake National Recreation Area, part of the North Cascades National Park Complex (National Park Service). Jack Mountain itself and the Nohokomeen Glacier are in the Pasayten Wilderness on the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest.
access.passRequired: None - no pass or permit is reported to be required for the East Bank Trailhead approach.

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades National Park Complex backcountry permit (covers Ross Lake NRA) - quota, not free
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount. Cross-country climbing camps need a permit for the zone you camp in.

road.name: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) to the East Bank Trailhead, milepost 138
road.status: Paved highway with roadside trailhead parking on the north side near MP 138. No pass required to park. Ross Lake Resort water taxi is an alternative access from the lake.
road.driveNote: SR 20 east from Marblemount and Newhalem to milepost 138, roughly 18.5 miles east of Newhalem. The trailhead is signed for the East Bank Trail / Panther Creek; from the lot a short descent leads to the Ruby Creek bridge.
road.seasonalGate: SR 20 closes each winter between the Ross Dam gate (MP 134) and the Silver Star gate (MP 171), typically late November/early December to mid-April or early May; in heavy years the gates fall back to Newhalem (MP 120) and Early Winters (MP 178). Because the best conditions on this route are in spring, early-season parties often bike about 4 miles from the MP 134 gate to the trailhead. The 2026 opening was delayed to June 14 by December 2025 flood damage.

climate.fall: Broken glacier and bare ice; not a viable objective on this aspect.
climate.spring: The season. A cold window in May offers the best combination of long days, a filled-in bergschrund and a stable snowpack; parties consistently report that early May beats late May and that June is too late.
climate.summer: The bergschrund opens, the glacier breaks up and the headwall loses its snow. Not the season for this route, though the mountain's south side comes into condition.
climate.winter: Documented winter ascents exist (including a late-January climb), but they involve biking and skiing in from the highway gate, mixed climbing through a cliff band, and full avalanche and cornice hazard management.
climate.typical: A deep, shaded, north-facing cirque that holds winter conditions long after the south side of the mountain has dried out. Cold clear nights give the overnight refreeze the route depends on.
climate.forecastZone: For avalanche information NWAC's West Slopes North is the nearest named zone; because this is a spring snow route on a big north face, the NWAC forecast plus your own observations of overnight refreeze are the operative data.

emergency.notes: No cell coverage anywhere on this route. Carry a satellite messenger or PLB, and be aware the north cirque's sky view is poor - move onto open glacier or the ridge to send. Ross Lake Resort boat traffic on the lake is the nearest regular human presence. Plan for self-rescue: an evacuation from the Nohokomeen cirque would take days.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Rd, Marblemount, WA 98267 - 360-854-7245. This is the permit office for the Ross Lake NRA portion of the approach.
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth United General Medical Center, 2000 Hospital Dr, Sedro-Woolley, WA 98284 - (360) 856-6021, 24-hour emergency department.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911; Whatcom County Sheriff non-emergency dispatch 360-676-6911. Whatcom County Search & Rescue is dispatched through the Sheriff's Office.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: May, in a cold spell, while the headwall snow is continuous and the bergschrund is still bridged

May.reason: Long days, a still-bridged bergschrund and a continuous headwall; SR 20 usually opens mid-month, and a cold window keeps the 55-degree snow firm.

July.reason: The schrund is typically open, the lower glacier is broken up and the headwall snow is sun-rotted; this is not a summer route.

June.reason: The bergschrund opens quickly, often to a single bridge, and warm afternoons load the headwall with wet slides.

April.reason: Snowpack is continuous from about 4,800 ft and the schrund is closed, but the highway is usually still gated, adding a bike leg from MP 134.

March.reason: SR 20 is still gated at MP 134, so parties bike or ski in; winter slab and cornice hazard on the headwall is still high.

approach_variants.name: East Bank Trail on foot from milepost 138, leaving it at May Creek
camps: High camp below the Nohokomeen Glacier
approach_variants.notes: Park at the East Bank Trailhead near milepost 138 at about 1,800 ft. The trail drops immediately to the bridge over Ruby Creek and then runs north along Ross Lake, mostly flat and fast, to the May Creek camp. This is the whole of the easy walking. At May Creek leave the trail and climb west to north-west, staying loosely between the creeks on the mountain's west side. Cliff bands start around 3,200 ft and are threaded on boot and game trails rather than climbed; snow generally begins around 4,800 to 5,000 ft. Three miles or so of that work reaches a flat camp just over 5,200 ft below the toe of the ice. Strong parties carry a second camp onto the upper glacier near 7,400 ft, which shortens summit day considerably.
approach_variants.season: Late May through July while the headwall is still a snow climb; the highway gate closes the season at both ends
hazards: steep brushy timber with cliff bands from about 3,200 ft, far worse to reverse than to ascend
crevasses on the Nohokomeen Glacier, thinly bridged late in the season
sustained steep snow on the headwall itself, with a long runout onto the glacier below
rockfall and icefall off the wall once the sun reaches it
a two to four day commitment with no quick way off the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The timber belt is the navigation, the glacier toe is the arrival. Leaving May Creek you are looking for weaknesses, not a line: the cliff bands from about 3,200 ft up are passed on boot and game trails that thread left and right, so a section that forces you to climb rock means you have pushed into the band rather than around it. The reliable signal that you are through is underfoot rather than overhead - continuous snow starting somewhere near 4,800 to 5,000 ft, and above that the timber gives out onto open ground.

The camp is a flat bench, not a viewpoint. Just over 5,200 ft the ground levels into a flat bench directly below the toe of the ice. If you are on sloping heather with the ice still out of sight above you, keep going; if you are already on the ice you have walked past the bench.

The headwall is above the glacier, not at its toe. From the bench the glacier runs up in front of you at an easy angle for a long way before anything steepens. The route's steep ground is the wall at the head of that ice, directly beneath the summit. If you are roping up and swinging tools within minutes of leaving camp, you are on a serac or a crevasse wall low on the glacier, not on the headwall. The headwall is only reached after the whole gentle bowl has been crossed and the ground ahead of you rears up as one continuous face rather than a series of rolls.

A cross-check at the top of the ice: the summit should be directly above the headwall, not off to one side. If the wall in front of you tops out on a shoulder with more mountain visible beyond it, you have drifted around the bowl.

bivy.notes: Designated camp on the East Bank Trail about 8 miles from the East Bank trailhead, where climbers leave the trail for the north side of Jack Mountain. It can also be reached by water taxi. Used as a first night or as the camp on the way out.

approach_variants.notes: The resort at the south end of Ross Lake runs a water taxi that will drop parties on the eastern shore, which removes most of the flat trail miles and turns the approach into the off-trail climb alone. It has to be booked ahead and the schedule and drop points change, so confirm directly before building a trip around it. The trade is that you are committed to a pickup time on a lake with no road out, so build slack into the plan rather than into the summit day.
approach_variants.season: Same window as the trail approach, but only once the boat service is running for the year
hazards: fixed pickup times on a lake with no road out
the same steep brushy cliff-banded timber belt above the shore
arriving late enough that the timber belt is done in the dark
crevasses on the glacier above
no reliable communication once off the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the landing the first task is to get onto the trail and find may creek - the East Bank Trail runs along this shore and the departure point is the creek, not a bearing. Once you leave the trail at May Creek every marker is identical to the walk-in variant: cliff bands from around 3,200 ft passed on game trails, continuous snow near 4,800 to 5,000 ft, and the flat bench just over 5,200 ft below the toe of the ice.

The one thing the boat changes is your margin, not your route. Parties dropped late in the day have started the timber belt in fading light, which is where the cliff bands become genuinely dangerous, because the passages through them are found by eye. If you cannot reach open ground above the bands in daylight, camp low rather than commit to the belt.

The negative marker is the same: if the ground ahead of you steepens into rock rather than easing onto snow, you are in a cliff band and should traverse to find the boot track rather than force it.

approach_variants.name: Before the highway opens: the gate at milepost 134
approach_variants.notes: The highway closes each winter between the gate west of the trailhead and a second gate far to the east, and reopens somewhere between mid-April and early summer depending on the year's damage and snowpack. Parties wanting the headwall in condition have started at the closed gate and covered the road on bikes or skis to the trailhead before starting the walk in. Everything above that is unchanged, except that the snow line is far lower and the timber belt may go faster on skis than it does on foot in summer.
approach_variants.season: Late winter and early spring, before the highway is cleared, when the headwall holds its best snow
hazards: avalanche terrain through the timber belt and on the glacier approach in early season
a long road section on bike or ski before the trip proper starts
short daylight and cold, with a committing position
cornices on the upper mountain
the road gate opening date moves year to year and can strand a plan
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The road section is navigation-free; the approach still starts at may creek. Ride or ski the closed highway to the trailhead near milepost 138 and pick up the East Bank Trail there. The departure from the trail is the creek, as in summer.

What changes is where the snow starts. In this window continuous snow is likely to begin well below the 4,800 to 5,000 ft line that summer parties describe, which means the cliff bands between roughly 3,200 ft and there are being crossed on snow rather than on game trails. A band that would be walked around in August may be a loaded slope in April. If the passage you would normally take through a band is a smooth, wind-loaded ramp rather than a boot track, treat it as avalanche terrain and not as a route.

The flat bench just over 5,200 ft below the glacier toe may be buried and unrecognisable as a bench; in that case the arrival marker is the change of angle where the ground stops climbing and the ice begins running away ahead of you toward the wall.

backups.name: East Peak (Standard Route)
backups.season: Jul–Sep (best); possible into June or October in low-snow years
gear: Glacier travel kit: rope and crevasse rescue gear
Light rock rack (small cams/nuts) and a few slings for the 5.4 step
Northwest Forest Pass for trailhead parking
hazards: Crevasses on the Triad and Eldorado Glaciers, especially with thin or icy early/late-season cover
Loose rock and rockfall potential on the class 4-5.4 step near East Triad Col, particularly with other parties above
Complex terrain among the three closely spaced Triad summits that is easy to misjudge in fog or whiteout
Steep, brushy off-trail terrain between about 5,400 ft and Sibley Creek Pass
Heavy, wet Cascade snowpack creates high avalanche danger on the Sibley Creek approach slopes outside summer
backups.overview: The Triad is a cluster of three rocky summits (west, middle, and east peaks, all within roughly 80 ft of each other in height) on the southwest ridge extension of Eldorado Peak, rising above the remote, glaciated Marble Creek cirque in North Cascades National Park. Composed of granodioritic orthogneiss, the peaks were first climbed in 1949 by Dick Eilertsen, Dick Lowery, Dick Scales, and Don Wilde -- a party of three climbers all named Dick, who first called the massif the 'Three Dicks' before the tamer 'Triad' stuck. It lies about 2 miles southwest of Eldorado Peak (~8,873 ft) and offers views toward Dorado Needle and Early Morning Spire. Despite sitting right next to one of the North Cascades' most popular glacier climbs, the Triad itself is rarely ascended.
backups.beta: From the Hidden Lake Trail, leave the maintained tread to gain a heather-covered ridge, cross a small unnamed glacier on the peak's north side, and descend a steep, loose gully nicknamed the 'Drainage of Despair' to reach the base of the East Ridge. Climb ramps and a slabby section up and right to the ridge crest (an old rappel anchor marks easier ground above), then a short, exposed low-5th-class pinnacle pitch with sparse protection gains the true summit. The technical crux is a committing 4th-class move used to gain the ridge itself from a ledge system below.
backups.turnaround: On a remote peak with a long approach, set a turnaround that ensures a safe return before dark. Retreat if weather builds, as the exposed towers are no place for a storm.
backups.rock_grade: 5.0–5.4 (low 5th class); some parties rate the crux stiff 4th class instead
backups.rappels: Commonly 2 rappels of roughly 30m off anchors near the crux (rope + tagline useful); some parties downclimb instead
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: No reliable cell service should be expected on the approach or route; North Cascades National Park backcountry generally has little to no coverage, though isolated high ridgelines occasionally catch a weak signal. Do not rely on a phone for emergency communication — a satellite messenger or PLB is strongly recommended.
backups.descent: Reverse the route with a short rappel off the summit tower back to the approach.

waypoints.name: Hidden Lake Trailhead (FR-1540 / Sibley Creek Road)
waypoints.directions: From Marblemount, follow Cascade River Road (FR-15) for about 10.2 paved miles, then turn onto FR-1540, Sibley Creek Road, and grind out 4.5 miles of rough gravel to the small Hidden Lake Trailhead at about 3,600 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park. Many parties sleep at the trailhead the night before rather than driving in before dawn. No permit is needed for a day climb; only overnight camping inside the national park requires one. Road access and snow on the ridge and glacier edge are the seasonal gate, so plan on roughly July through September.

sectionBreakdown.fromTo: Car-to-car climb via Hidden Lake Trailhead

backups.detailed_rack: A light rack of cams to 2 inches, a set of nuts, several slings for the towers, and a 60m rope for the short step and rappel. Add ice axe and crampons for the approach.
pro_tips: Combine with Eldorado's Inspiration Glacier or West Arete route via the same Sibley Creek Pass approach to make efficient use of a multi-day glacier camp
Cross the Triad Glacier early in the day while the snow surface is firm to minimize crevasse-fall risk
watch_out: The Triad Glacier has been reported rock-hard under a thin snow layer in some conditions -- bring sharp crampons and be ready to belay short sections
Off-trail routefinding from about 5,400 ft to Sibley Creek Pass is difficult in poor visibility
There is no easy bail-out from East Triad Col other than re-crossing the glacier the way you came
backups.pro_needs: Protection on the short technical step is adequate in cracks and around horns, while the scrambling sections are largely unprotected. Comfort on exposed terrain matters more than a large rack.
backups.approach: From Marblemount, drive Cascade River Road (FR-15) about 10.2 paved miles, then turn onto FR-1540 (Sibley Creek Road) and follow its rough gravel surface 4.5 miles to the small Hidden Lake Trailhead (~3,600 ft; Northwest Forest Pass required to park). Hike Hidden Lake Trail #745 through forest and wildflower meadows to about 5,400 ft, where the maintained trail begins a long traverse; leave the trail here and climb steep meadow and heather slopes to 6,200-ft Sibley Creek Pass. From the pass, a boot path follows the crest of a grassy ridge before dropping onto the Triad Glacier, which is crossed -- often on rock-hard ice under a thin snow layer -- past all three Triad summits to East Triad Col. This is a full, long approach day (roughly 6+ miles with significant elevation gain and loss) and is typically done as part of a multi-day trip with a high camp near Sibley Creek Pass or on the glacier apron.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the route: downclimb the class 4-5.4 step from the East Peak back to East Triad Col, then re-cross the Triad Glacier roped up (watch for open crevasses, especially in late season) back to Sibley Creek Pass, and descend the boot path/meadows to Hidden Lake Trail #745 and the trailhead.
backups.bail: Retreat is reasonable by reversing the scramble and short rappel, though the long, complex approach must still be reversed regardless of how high you climbed.

pitch_detail.notes: From East Triad Col, scramble up broken, blocky terrain to a wide ledge that runs toward the peak's east ridge; the ledge has one or two exposed but avoidable moves, then a stiff, committing Class 4 step gains the crest of the ridge proper.

Follow the exposed east ridge to the base of the summit tower and climb a short, tricky 5.4 crack/step onto the highest block; descend from the same rap station with a single-rope rappel back to the ridge before reversing to the col.

itinerary.cal: No permit is needed for a day climb (only overnight camping in North Cascades NP requires one); Cascade River Road access and snow conditions on the ridge/glacier edge are the main seasonal gate, roughly July-September.

days.note: This is a long but standard single-day outing, not a backpack trip: parties drive to the Hidden Lake Trailhead (often sleeping at the trailhead the night before) and climb car-to-car via the Hidden Lake climbers' trail onto the ridge, then the East Ridge to the summit. Parties typically take roughly 6 hours up and ~10.5 hours round trip for a fit party, with one short rappel/4th-class step near the top.

climate.typical: A marine west-coast mountain climate: heavy, wet winter snowfall builds a deep, avalanche-prone snowpack, followed by a relatively short, drier climbing window in mid- to late summer. A small unnamed glacier feeds the Triad Glacier on the peak's north side.

bySeason.fall: Shortening days and the risk of early snow; glacier crevasses are typically most open and the glacier surface can be icy and hard.
bySeason.spring: Deep lingering snowpack can bury approach brush and bridge crevasses well, but avalanche danger remains elevated on the Sibley Creek Pass slopes.
bySeason.summer: Best climbing window; the Triad/Eldorado Glacier crossing is usually most stable early in the window, with crevasses opening progressively through August into September.
bySeason.winter: Heavy, wet snow loading creates high avalanche danger on the Sibley Creek approach slopes; not a realistic winter objective.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is essentially nonexistent in the Marble Creek/Eldorado cirque; carry a satellite communicator or PLB for emergencies.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very high - parties describe a long, sustained single-day push from the Hidden Lake Trailhead across brushy, off-trail terrain and a glacier crossing; expect a full mountain day of 10+ hours car-to-car
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Moderate-to-heavy - full glacier travel kit (rope, crevasse-rescue gear), a light rock rack, and a 60m rope; no overnight camping gear is needed for the standard single-day car-to-car push

partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced alpine climber/mountaineer with prior roped glacier-travel trips - not a suitable first alpine objective

July.reason: Within the season, but early July can still carry lingering snowpack and higher meltwater stream crossings on the approach; conditions generally firm up by mid-month.

August.reason: Center of the Mid-July through September window - most consolidated glacier conditions for the approach and driest brush, with the most stable weather window of the season.

September.reason: Still within the season; shorter days and cooler temps, with rising odds of early-season snow or storms later in the month given the afternoon-thunderstorm hazard.

weather.typical: Summer alpine weather typical of the North Cascades - generally the driest, most stable conditions of the year within the July-Sept window, consistent with the best-season/climate framing.
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are a hazard here; the exposed granite towers and summit step raise lightning and rockfall-from-storm risk, so early starts and a weather-watch turnaround plan are warranted.

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Consequential - loose blocks on the towers and an exposed summit step; a fall or rockfall incident on the summit block or towers would be serious given the remote, complex setting far from rescue access.

avalanche.zone: N/A - route is climbed July-Sept, outside NWAC's forecast season (NWAC issues zone forecasts roughly mid-November through mid-April only); no avalanche zone forecast applies during the climbing window

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Real hazard on the approach - 'crevasses and snow on the approach' across the glaciated terrain shared with the Eldorado access; roped glacier travel and crevasse-rescue readiness are required, especially earlier in the July-Sept window when snow bridges are less consolidated.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Marblemount, drive Cascade River Road (FR-15) about 10.2 paved miles, then turn onto FR-1540 (Sibley Creek Road) and follow its rough gravel surface 4.5 miles to the small Hidden Lake Trailhead (~3,600 ft; Northwest Forest Pass required to park).

approach_variants.name: Sibley Creek Pass and the north-side glacier
approach_variants.notes: From the Hidden Lake Trailhead hike the maintained trail through forest and wildflower meadows to about 5,400 ft, where it begins a long traverse; leave it there and climb steep meadow and heather to Sibley Creek Pass. From the pass a boot path follows a grassy ridge crest before dropping onto the small glacier on the peaks' north side, which is crossed past all three summits — often on rock-hard ice under a thin skin of snow — to the col at the east end. This is a full approach day and is normally done with a high camp near the pass or on the glacier apron.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July to September, gated by the gravel road in and by snow on the ridge and glacier edge
hazards: Hard ice under thin snow on the glacier crossing — crampons
A steep, loose gully of dirt and rock lying on top of steeper rock and heather drops to the base
Sparse protection on the short exposed pinnacle pitch to the true summit
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cross the small unnamed glacier on the north side and then find the descent, because the base of this ridge is below you, not above. The way down is a steep, loose gully of dirt and rock sitting on top of even steeper rock and heather — unpleasant enough that parties who have done it have given it a name — and it drops from the glacier edge to the foot of the ridge between the east summit and the main one. From the bottom, the climbing starts on ramps and a slabby section trending up and right toward the ridge crest. The proof you have picked the right line is an old rappel anchor on the crest, which marks where the ground eases above it; the committing fourth-class move used to pull onto the ridge from the ledge system below is the hardest thing on the route and it comes before that anchor, not after. If you are standing on the glacier looking for a way up, or you have not lost height since leaving the ice, you have not reached the base.

gear: a handful of slings for anchors
hazards: Rockfall from ridge due to exposed terrain and looser sections
Inclement weather develops rapidly, particularly afternoon thunderstorms
Sustained 5.6 climbing with exposure requires strong skills; fall protection essential
backups.overview: A cool 5.6 romp up exposed ridge combining fourth-class scrambling with short 5th-class sections. Similar commitment to North Ridge but slightly more technical. Half-day alpine objective from Boston Basin camps.
backups.beta: Approach as for Forbidden Peak from low camp (5,300 ft) or high camp (6,400 ft). Navigate toward South Ridge approach facing Forbidden Glacier. Route-finding less obvious than North Ridge; scout carefully. Follow exposed ridge combining fourth-class scrambling with short pitches of 5.6 climbing.
backups.turnaround: Start very early to ensure completion with safe daylight margin. If not at summit by mid-afternoon, retreat for safe descent.
backups.rappels: Descends via North Ridge: 1 rappel (~40 ft) from fixed slings
backups.face: South Ridge (left-hand skyline as seen from Boston Basin)
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).

backups.descent: Descend via same ridge or similar route depending on descent planning. Likely requires belayed sections and possible rappels.

backups.detailed_rack: A light alpine rack covers this route: a single set of cams from finger-size up to about 2in, with doubles in the common 0.5-1in range for the sustained low-5th ridge climbing and the 5.6 crux on pitch 3 (bypassing a gendarme on the right, on more solid but harder rock). Bring a set of stoppers/nuts too — the ridge is described as loose and lichen-covered in places, so smaller opportunistic nut/cam placements matter as much as a big piece. There is no fixed protection on-route except a single faded rap sling at the P2/P3 notch belay below the gendarme.
what_to_bring: ice axe, and crampons if there's residual snow in Forbidden Gully/Cat Scratch Gullies on the approach
approach shoes/light boots for scree and snowfield approach to Boston Basin
bivy/camp gear for the multi-day Boston Basin approach
pro_tips: Start very early to maximize daylight
South Ridge approach requires careful route-finding
Be confident in 5.6 climbing before attempting
Test holds carefully; rockfall hazard on exposed ridges
Establish solid anchors for crux sections
Watch cloud development; weather deteriorates rapidly
watch_out: Rockfall: exposed ridge means falling rock is hazard
Exposure: more sustained than North Ridge
Route-finding: South Ridge approach less obvious
Weather volatility: afternoon thunderstorms common
Descent exposure: plan carefully as you ascend
backups.pro_needs: Protection is moderate but not continuous — this is a broken, sometimes loose ridge crest rather than a clean crack system, so gear comes from natural placements as terrain allows rather than a splitter line. There is an abundance of loose, lichen-y rock, and belayers on pitch 2 should stay out of the fall line because of rockfall risk from parties above on the pitch 3 crux.
backups.best_season: July-August most stable. August typically driest. Snow may linger at high camp into July; September dry with possible large crevasses.
backups.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to Burlington, then WA-20 east through Marblemount, and turn onto Cascade River Road, following its paved-then-gravel surface about 21.7 miles to a small pullout at 3,200 ft that marks the unmaintained Boston Basin Trailhead (a different stop, about a mile or so up-road of the Eldorado trailhead, and just before the road's end at Cascade Pass). From there a steep, unmaintained climbers' path follows the old Diamond Mine roadbed briefly before climbing hard, crossing several streams, and breaking above treeline (~5,300 ft) to reach the popular Boston Basin high camp around 6,400 ft — roughly 3-4 miles one-way with about 3,000-3,300 ft of elevation gain. From camp, West Ridge climbers continue cross-country over the glacier to a couloir that gains the ridge crest. Because Boston Basin is a high-demand cross-country camping zone in North Cascades National Park, overnight parties need a wilderness permit; a portion of peak-season (mid-May to mid-October) slots can be reserved in advance via Recreation.gov's early-access lottery, with the remainder issued as limited first-come, first-served walk-up permits. For this specific route: from Boston Basin high camp, a short approach up into the Forbidden Peak zone reaches this minor summit; North and South Ridge differ only in which side of the formation is climbed from the same camp.
backups.descent_text: Descend exposed ridge via Class 4 scrambling and short 5.6 downclimbing. Depending on party confidence, rappel may be used for crux section. Reverse route-finding back to camp.
backups.bail: Exposed nature makes retreat more committing than North Ridge. If weather deteriorates, descend carefully via ridge to rejoin approach.

pitch_detail.notes: Leave the snowfield, move right, then head straight up to reach the ridge crest.
Follow the crest to a small notch at the foot of a gendarme; belay here, out of the fall line of the next pitch.
Crux. Get round the gendarme on its right side, where the rock is firmer, then climb back onto the crest.
Airy ridge climbing up to the cockscomb. Loose and lichen-covered rock in places.
On to the summit; this stretch goes most smoothly as two or three short pitches.

backups.itinerary: Day 1: Drive to the Boston Basin trailhead and hike in to high camp (~6,400 ft). Day 2: Early start, approach via snowfields to the base of the South Ridge, climb the 5 pitches to the top, then descend via the North Ridge back to camp.
