approach_logistics.trailhead: Boston Basin climbers' trailhead (Cascade River Road)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to Burlington, then WA-20 east through Marblemount, and turn onto Cascade River Road, following its paved-then-gravel surface about 21.7 miles to a small pullout at 3,200 ft that marks the unmaintained Boston Basin Trailhead (a different, lower stop than the Eldorado trailhead a mile or so up-road, and just before the road's end at Cascade Pass).

backups.rope_note: Standard multi-pitch 5.6 alpine granite route in Boston Basin; well-protected cracks/corners take a light alpine rack.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin high camp
approach_variants.notes: From the small pullout on Cascade River Road, take the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the old mine roadbed, across several streams and out above treeline to the Boston Basin camps. The formation is visible and easily picked out from the basin, and the climb is a half-day outing on light packs from camp. Overnight parties need a wilderness permit for the basin.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn, from an established camp in the basin
hazards: Route-finding here is markedly less obvious than on the other side of the formation — scout the line from the basin before committing
Exposed ridge with short fifth-class steps between fourth-class scrambling
Glacier and snow travel to reach the foot of the crest
approach_variants.baseFinding: The formation is the cockscomb standing on the divide between the upper Forbidden basin and the Torment basin with its glacier — a small, sharply notched crest that reads as an M from below, which is where its name comes from, and it is unmistakable once you are up out of the basin. Two skylines run down off it and the whole question is which one you are under. The right-hand skyline is the other route on the formation; the left-hand one is this climb. The negative marker is exact and easy to check on the ground: the right-hand route is entered from a notch on the right of that skyline, and from that notch it gives three or four pitches of fourth class to the foot of a tower and then one short pitch to its top. If you are standing in a notch on the right-hand side of the formation looking at a tower, you are on the other route. This ridge is gained round the far end of the crest, is the longer and less obvious of the two, and parties consistently find the route-finding on it the harder part of the day.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are no longer free — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

backups.name: Northeast Ridge (2003 Variation)
gear: ice axe for early-season approach snow
hazards: Shattered, friable andesite giving both loose holds and unreliable protection — the defining characteristic of every route on this peak.
An explicitly unstable Class 4+ section low on the route that must be crossed to reach the good climbing.
PG13 protection: significant fall consequences in places.
Rockfall onto belayers from a ridge line littered with loose blocks.
Six pitches at 5.9 plus a route-finding descent make benightment a genuine risk on a short-day trip.
Summer convection over the Cascade crest and a fully exposed position.
No cell coverage and a remote, gravel-access trailhead: slow rescue response.
backups.overview: A six-pitch, 1,000-foot Grade III 5.9 variation that branches off where the original Northeast Ridge finishes its first pitch, taking a left-facing corner with a vertical crack through yellow-speckled rock and roofs. The best pitch on the route is a well-protected 5.7/5.8 crack; the second pitch's scary, unstable Class 4+ rock is what holds the route back.
backups.beta: Put up by Mike Preiss and Mark Bunker in 2003. It starts where the original Northeast Ridge route ends its first pitch. From there, traverse left and up through scary, unstable Class 4+ rock on a short pitch, aiming for a left-hand vertical crack in a left-facing corner identified by yellow-speckled rock with roofs above. The crux third pitch follows that crack and exits over its left side — the route's best pitch, rated 5.7/5.8 and well protected. Above, the rock eases and parties navigate upward through variations, with a short difficult left-leaning crack at 5.9+ before moderate terrain leads to the summit area. It carries a PG13 protection rating and would deserve a higher star rating were it not for the precarious second pitch.
backups.turnaround: Fix a turnaround before you start the second pitch. The considerations here are the PG13 protection rating and the unstable Class 4+ traverse pitch, which are both far more dangerous when hurried; the fact that six pitches at 5.9 on shattered andesite go slowly; and the unfamiliar, loose south-side descent that has to be completed in daylight. If the crux corner is not behind you with most of the day still available, retreat.
backups.rappels: No established rappel line; descend the south side. Carry spare slings and rings to build bail anchors if you need to retreat off the lower pitches. Doubled ropes make retreat from mid-route far more practical.
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage at the trailhead, on the approach, or on the northeast side of the peak. Plan to be out of contact and carry a satellite messenger or PLB. Nearest dependable service is toward Roslyn and Cle Elum.
backups.descent: Descend the south side via the ordinary Southwest Face route to Cathedral Pass.

waypoints.name: Cathedral Rock Trailhead (Trail #1345)
waypoints.directions: Leave I-90 at Exit 80 and follow SR-903 north through Roslyn and Ronald for about 14.8 miles, then continue roughly 12.3 miles on the gravel Cle Elum Valley Road / FR 4330 and the NF-153 spur to the Cathedral Rock trailhead for Trail #1345, at about 3,350 ft. Sign the free wilderness permit at the register before you start walking. There is no cell coverage here, and between that and the remote gravel access any rescue will be slow, so leave your plan with somebody before you drive in.

backups.detailed_rack: Published descriptions specify medium rock protection up to 4+ inches, runners and a helmet. In practice: a single set of nuts, cams from small through 4 inches (with the larger sizes for the left-facing corner and the left-leaning crack), and a generous set of alpine draws and double-length runners for slinging blocks and horns and for keeping drag manageable on a wandering line. Two ropes, or one 60m plus a tag, so that bailing from the middle of the route is possible. Spare slings and rap rings. A helmet is explicitly called for.

backups.pro_needs: The route is rated PG13. The crux third pitch — the vertical crack in the left-facing corner — is described as well protected and is the best pitch on the climb; the problem is the short second pitch of scary, unstable Class 4+ rock leading to it, where the protection and the rock quality are both poor. The short 5.9+ left-leaning crack higher up is the other place where gear matters. Elsewhere the rock eases and the climbing is moderate. Sling solid features in preference to placing cams in the fractured andesite.
backups.best_season: Late July through September. The northeast aspect stays in shade and dries slowly, so give the route time after any rain, and expect snow on the approach terrain into July. Late August and September give the driest rock and the coldest, most stable air — worth waiting for on a route where the protection is already marginal.
backups.approach: Drive to the Cathedral Rock trailhead (Trail #1345, ~3,350 ft) via I-90 Exit 80, SR-903 north through Roslyn and Ronald about 14.8 miles, then 12.3 miles of gravel Cle Elum Valley Road / FR 4330 and the NF-153 spur. Sign the free wilderness permit at the register. Hike trail #1345 past Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake, ~4,850 ft) at 2.5 miles to the Cathedral Pass / PCT junction at 5,550 ft, 4 miles in. From there the northeast side is reached the same way as the Northeast Buttress: cut across the meadow to the stand of trees (a good gear cache), then traverse under the east face across talus toward the northeast side of the peak. Note that this route begins from the top of the original Northeast Ridge route's first pitch.
backups.descent_text: From the summit area, descend the south side rather than reversing the ridge. Scramble the Class 2-3 crest southwest to the top of the Southwest Face crux, make one or two rappels using the rock horn with fixed slings and rings (inspect and back it up), downclimb the main gully — the loosest ground of the day — and contour southeast across talus and heather to Cathedral Pass. Pick up any cached gear on the way back around to the trail. Trip reports on the neighbouring Northeast Buttress describe the south side as having more frequent traffic and correspondingly less loose rock, which is why it is the universal descent for the peak. Allow 2-3 hours summit to pass, plus 1.5-2 hours down trail #1345.
backups.bail: Retreat is realistic on the lower half. From the tricky second pitch and the base of the crux corner you can rappel from gear back to the original Northeast Ridge start and down. Once above the crux and into the easing ground, continuing to the summit and descending the south side is faster and safer than reversing loose 5.9 terrain. Carry spare slings and rings so you can leave anchors without stripping your rack.

Above the crux corner the rock eases; parties navigate upward through variations.

backups.itinerary: Long day trip: trailhead by 5am, Cathedral Pass and gear cache by 8:30am, on the route by mid-morning, six pitches through the middle of the day, summit early-to-mid afternoon, south-side descent and hike out — 12-14 hours car to car. A camp at Nosh Nosh Wahtum or Cathedral Pass on the night before converts it into a comfortable two-day trip and is the more common approach for a 5.9 alpine route this far from the road.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
Be clear about what you are looking for: this route's base is the top of somebody else's first pitch. You find the original Northeast Ridge start — the short steep snowfield on the northeast side, exiting left into the moat rather than right onto the harder ledges — climb its first pitch, and only then are you at the beginning of the 2003 line.

The feature that proves you are on the variation and not on the original, and this is the one to memorise, is yellow-speckled rock. From the top of that first pitch, traverse left and up over a short pitch of genuinely unstable class 4+ ground, aiming for a left-hand vertical crack in a left-facing corner, identified by yellow-speckled rock with roofs above it. Yellow speckles plus roofs above a left-facing corner is the target; nothing else on this side of the peak reads that way.

The confirmation is the third pitch: it climbs that crack and exits over its left side. It is the best pitch on the route, 5.7 to 5.8 and well protected — which is worth knowing precisely because everything below it is not. If pitch three is poorly protected choss, you are not in the corner you wanted.

A higher check: above, the rock eases, and a short difficult left-leaning crack at 5.9+ comes before moderate terrain to the summit.

And the honest warning that belongs in a base finding here: the pitch you must cross to reach the good climbing is described by the first-ascent party as scary and unstable. It is rated PG13, and the route would carry more stars if not for that second pitch. Knowing that in advance is what stops a party assuming they are off route when the ground feels wrong.

backups.overview: Davis Peak is a steep, forested-then-rocky summit directly north of Gorge Lake in North Cascades National Park, just south of the Picket Range. Originally called Stetattle Peak, it was renamed in 1904 by the Reaburn survey party for the Davis family, early homesteaders who ran a roadhouse for trappers and travelers near present-day Diablo. The mountain is best known among climbers for its huge Northeast Face, which drops roughly 5,250 ft in one horizontal mile — one of the two steepest such drops in the contiguous U.S. The standard route climbs the peak's southwest side: a long, sustained, mostly off-trail approach gaining close to 6,000 ft, capped by a Class 3 (occasionally brief Class 4 on wet slab) scramble to the summit.
backups.beta: Two variants converge near the summit block: the classic South Ridge/South Buttress (Class 2-3, occasional Class 4 slab moves, with an exposed ~65° step-down at a notch below 5,800 ft on the old line) and the now-more-popular SW Face snow route (steepest snow ~40°+), which was pioneered as a ski descent and downgraded the peak to a 'non-technical' objective when snow-covered. Either way, the approach through the lower Gorge Creek forest — with cliff bands around 2,400 ft and 2,800 ft, dense alder/vine-maple, and (below ~4,000 ft on some lines) 2015-burn deadfall — is the real crux of the day.
backups.turnaround: Given the multi-thousand-foot, route-finding-heavy bushwhack approach and an equally long descent, set a firm turnaround time that guarantees clearing the brushy forest sections and any snow/rock scrambling before dark; do not push for the summit if you are already behind schedule on the approach.
backups.rock_grade: Class 3 with a few Class 4 moves (the forested bluffs low on the route)
backups.rappels: None. The party that climbed it in April 2026 carried a 30 m rope specifically for the forested bluffs, on the strength of other trip reports stressing the difficulty there, and never took it out of the pack — they cached it with the harnesses at the last rocky island before the snow. A short rope remains reasonable insurance for the bluffs and the one short vertical icy step on the upper face.
backups.comms: Assume no coverage. The route starts in the Skagit gorge at the Gorge Creek bridge and North Cascades National Park advises that cell service is limited or unavailable through its backcountry. Carry a satellite messenger or PLB. Newhalem and Diablo, the Seattle City Light company towns a few highway miles either side, are the nearest places to raise help by telephone; the Wilderness Information Center at Marblemount is the nearest staffed park facility.
backups.descent: Reverse the ascent route down the south ridge/buttress to the ~5,700 ft saddle and back down the Gorge Creek drainage. Stay well clear of the peak's Northeast side — its cliffs drop roughly 5,250 ft in one horizontal mile, among the most consequential terrain traps in the range if the party drifts off-route.
obj_haz: isothermal snow collapsing into boulder voids
summer cornices on the summit ridge

waypoints.name: Gorge Creek Overlook pull-off
waypoints.note: Parking pull-off on SR 20 near the Gorge Creek bridge, about 2.6 mi east of Newhalem; cross the highway bridge over Gorge Creek to start the off-trail ascent.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 east from Newhalem about 2.6 miles to the Gorge Creek Overlook pull-off at the bridge. Nothing above the overlook is a numbered or maintained trail, and there is no reliable water past the lower forest, so fill up at Gorge Creek before starting.

waypoints.name: Lower cliff band
waypoints.note: First of two brushy cliff bands on the steep forest ascent; bypass on the right (south) side per the standard line.
waypoints.directions: Cross the footbridge over Gorge Creek, leave the overlook path immediately, and start straight up the forested south-southwest flank on boot-track, cairns and game trails. The lower forest is steep and brushy and partly inside a 2015 burn, so expect deadfall; an animal-path line through the open timber is generally the fastest way through. Near 2,400 ft the first cliff band blocks the fall line — work right around it.

waypoints.name: Upper cliff band
waypoints.note: Second cliff band above the first; stay right through mixed forest and brush to avoid exposed rock.
waypoints.directions: Above the first band the steep timber continues and the second cliff band arrives only about 400 ft higher. Work right again through mixed forest and brush rather than trying to force a line up the rock.

waypoints.name: Vine maple / open timber band
waypoints.note: Route opens into more travelable open timber with vine maple and occasional animal paths after the steep lower forest slog.
waypoints.directions: Keep grinding up steep timber to roughly 3,600-3,800 ft, where a brushy gully and intermittent animal paths lead into more open woods and the travel finally eases. This is the longest and least pleasant stretch of the day and there is no water on it.

waypoints.name: Snow-filled gully
waypoints.note: Partially snow-filled gully marking the transition from forest to the upper talus/snow terrain; can hold snow into midsummer.
waypoints.directions: A couple of hundred feet higher the forest gives out at a gully that commonly holds snow well into midsummer. Early season this is where the axe and crampons come out; later in the year it is bare and loose.

waypoints.name: Talus draw
waypoints.note: Narrow talus draw leading up into the alpine snowfields below the south ridge.
waypoints.directions: Follow the gully up into a narrow talus draw around 4,500 ft that leads clear of the trees. Granite slabs and alpine snowfields start around 4,800-4,850 ft and the angle eases as the ground flattens onto the crest of the southwest ridge.

waypoints.name: South Davis Saddle
waypoints.note: Broad saddle on the south ridge, about 4.4 hrs from the trailhead; flattest ground on the route for a break or bivy, and the gain point for the summit ridge/buttress.
waypoints.directions: Climb snow and talus up the crest to the broad saddle at about 5,700-5,800 ft. Stay left/north of Point 5,872, the subpeak on the east ridge — its slopes have turned parties back with avalanche-prone snow in shoulder-season conditions. Reckon on 4 to 4.5 hours from the car to here for a fit party.

waypoints.name: Davis Peak
waypoints.note: True summit via Class 2-3 rock buttress with slime-coated slabs near the top and a corniced south ridge crest just below.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle the inviting line is the wide-open snow slopes leading to the east summit ridge, and it is a trap: those slopes close out at an impassable step roughly 300 ft below the top, and the retreat costs hours and a thousand feet of regain. Take the rock buttress instead, climbing its right flank — it looks steep and loose from below but goes at Class 2-3. Near the top a short 3rd-class chimney and a band of mossy, slime-coated slabs are the last obstacle, and the slabs can be turned by traversing hard left. The south ridge crest just under the summit can carry a cornice.

backups.detailed_rack: This is a scramble, not a roped rock route, and most parties climb it with no rack at all. In early-season or winter conditions, when the south ridge/SW Face holds steep snow (up to roughly 60-65°), bring an ice axe and crampons; a short (30m) rope with a few slings and a picket or two can be useful for a running belay across a moat or for protecting the exposed step at the old south-ridge notch.
what_to_bring: gaiters and brush-resistant clothing for alder bushwhacking

Carry an axe early season for lingering snow

The lower slopes burned in the 2015 Goodell Creek Fire - expect standing deadfall and increased brush; check recent trip reports for current conditions

backups.pro_needs: Class 2-3 scrambling on the approach and upper mountain, with brief Class 4 moves on wet or snow-covered slab reported by some parties near the top; no fixed rock protection is placed on the standard summer route. A helmet is worth carrying for the loose, broken terrain and for moat/cornice sections when snow lingers.
backups.best_season: Late July through mid-September gives the most reliable snow-free scrambling on the upper mountain and summit ridge; snow, moats, and cornices can linger into July on the shadier saddle and upper gullies. Some parties instead climb it in late May-June as a steep snow route while the approach brush is still snow-covered, and it has been climbed in winter during stable high-pressure windows by strong, experienced parties.
backups.approach: From the Gorge Creek Overlook pull-off on Highway 20 (about 1,100 ft, roughly 2.6 miles/4.2 km east of Newhalem), cross the metal footbridge over Gorge Creek and immediately leave the maintained overlook trail — there is no numbered or maintained trail beyond the bridge, so the rest of the approach is off-trail route-finding by boot-track, cairns, and game trails up Davis Peak's south/southwest flank. The lower forest (partly within a 2015 burn) is steep and brushy with deadfall and blowdown; an animal-path line generally holds up through open timber. Around 2,400-2,800 ft, cliff bands force a bypass (parties generally work right); continue up steep timber to roughly 3,600-3,800 ft, where a brushy gully and intermittent animal paths lead through more open woods. Near 4,000 ft a partly snow-filled gully, and around 4,500 ft a talus draw, mark the transition out of forest; granite slabs and alpine snowfields begin around 4,800-4,850 ft, where the angle eases as the terrain flattens onto the crest of the southwest ridge. Stay left/north of Point 5,872 (a subpeak on Davis's east ridge, sometimes called "Little Davie," ~6,240 ft) rather than committing to its slopes - multiple parties have found avalanche-prone snow there in shoulder-season conditions and turned back - and climb snow/talus to the broad notch/saddle at roughly 5,700-5,800 ft on the south ridge (about 4-4.5 hours from the car for a fit party). There is no reliable water past the lower forest, so fill up at Gorge Creek near the trailhead. Total distance is roughly 6-8 miles round trip with about 5,900 ft of gain from trailhead to the 7,054 ft summit, almost all of it off-trail through brush, talus, and low-5th-class-adjacent terrain. A longer alternate approach follows the primitive Stetattle Creek Trail about 2 miles from Diablo, then leaves the trail, drops about 200 ft to ford Stetattle Creek, and climbs the peak's north/west side - but the Stetattle Creek Trail is fully closed by NPS due to 2023 Sourdough Fire damage (standing dead trees/debris), a long-term closure with no end date given on the park's fire-closures page updated September 14, 2026, so this alternate is not usable while it stands; plan on the Gorge Creek Overlook approach instead.
backups.descent_text: Descend the same southwest ridge/south buttress line back to the 5,700-5,800 ft saddle, then drop the forested southwest flank back toward Gorge Creek. This is fundamentally a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route - most parties, including at least one documented winter ascent, downclimb the entire way with careful footing rather than pulling out a rope; ropework is not standard on the summer scramble. That said, the upper south buttress has a short band of slime-coated, mossy slabs just below the summit ridge, plus a lower cliff band further down the buttress, that some parties choose to rappel instead of downclimb, especially when wet: expect at most one or two short, single-strand rappels (a 30-60 m rope is more than enough for either) off whatever natural anchor is available - a tree, horn, or sling around a block, as there are no bolted or fixed anchors reported anywhere on this route. Below the buttress, glissade or plunge-step the snow gully/talus draw back through about 4,500 ft, then descend the same brushy, deadfall-choked forest line (partly in the 2015 burn) through the cliff-band bypass around 2,400-2,800 ft and back down to the Gorge Creek footbridge and Highway 20. Watch footing on the steep forest sections (parties report significant knee strain) and stay off snow above Point 5,872 or the peak's steep east-facing terrain, which can carry cornices and avalanche hazard well into the season.
backups.bail: Retreat down the southwest slopes at most points.

access.fees: $10/person/night + a flat $6 nonrefundable reservation fee (charged mid-May–early Oct only; free the rest of the year). No separate climbing fee — North Cascades NP entrance itself is free.
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Leave No Trace; this is an off-trail route with no established campsites - camp on durable surfaces (rock, snow, or gravel) where possible. NPS backcountry rules require cross-country camping at least 1/2 mile from any maintained trail and out of sight of it. A permit is required only for overnight camping, not for a single-day scramble.
access.permit: No permit is needed for a day scramble. A NPS Wilderness Permit is required for overnight camping: reserve on Recreation.gov, watch the mandatory orientation video, then email noca_wilderness@nps.gov up to 3 days before the trip, or get a walk-up permit in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount. Summer-season (mid-May-early October) backcountry camping fees are $10 per person plus a $6 nonrefundable reservation fee (youth 15 and under free); no camping fee is charged early October-mid-May.
access.closures: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) closes for the season in late November/early December and typically doesn't fully reopen until mid-to-late April (sometimes May in heavy-snow years) - check WSDOT's SR 20 pass report before driving. The Gorge Creek Overlook/Diablo trailhead area sits between the highway's two winter closure gates (Newhalem, milepost 120, and Ross Dam Trailhead/Silver Star, milepost 134/171), so it is among the first sections to lose road access as the highway closes and one of the last to reopen. The alternate Stetattle Creek Trail (the north/west approach via Diablo) is fully closed - not just historically closure-prone - due to standing dead trees and debris from the 2023 Sourdough Fire; NPS lists the entire trail as a long-term closure, with no end date given, on its fire-closures page updated September 14, 2026. Do not plan on this alternate approach until NPS lifts the closure; use the standard Gorge Creek Overlook approach instead.

access.passRequired: None. Davis Peak's trailheads (Gorge Creek Overlook, Stetattle Creek/Diablo) are within North Cascades National Park/Ross Lake National Recreation Area, which charges no entrance fee and requires no day-use parking pass. A Northwest Forest Pass is only needed at trailheads on adjacent national forest land elsewhere along SR 20 (e.g., Rainy Lake, Blue Lake near Washington Pass) - not at this trailhead.

crowds.peakTraffic: Rarely climbed even in peak summer months; described by multiple trip-report sources as 'almost unknown by climbers, let alone tourists'
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Likely fewer than 10-15 parties per season; no formal visitor counts exist for this objective

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong - long approach combining trail and cross-country travel with substantial elevation gain, brush, and deadfall in the lower zone
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Typically an overnight pack (20-35 lb) for a backcountry camp given the long approach; a very long single-push day is possible only for strong, fast parties

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long - typically a full-day approach (trail plus significant cross-country travel), often warranting a backcountry camp rather than a single push
requiredSkills: Class 3 scrambling on loose, broken rock
route-finding on trail-less, unmarked terrain
bushwhacking / off-trail navigation through alders and deadfall
early-season snow travel and basic self-arrest if attempting before the approach fully clears
sound judgment in thunderstorm-prone exposed terrain
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced scrambler comfortable with sustained, unmarked Class 3 terrain on loose/broken rock, plus significant off-trail route-finding; not a beginner objective

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September, once approach snow has melted out;

July.reason: Approach snow is often still lingering in shaded gullies and on the upper mountain early in the month; brushy lower approach can still be wet

August.reason: Most reliable window - approach typically fully melted out, driest rock, most stable access along the highway corridor

September.reason: Stable early in the month with continued dry rock; increasing chance of early-season snow and shortening daylight later in the month

weather.typical: Westside North Cascades climate - wet with lingering snow at elevation even into summer
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are common in mid-to-late summer

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Loose rock and route-finding on broken, unmarked upper-mountain terrain are the primary consequence-of-a-slip concerns; the long, trail-less approach through brush, deadfall, and bluffs compounds route-finding risk before the scramble even begins, and any residual early-season snow adds fall exposure on steep sections

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble route; no NWAC forecast zone specifically covers Davis Peak, and this route is normally climbed outside the snowpack season

approach_variants.name: Gorge Creek: straight up, and the 3,800 ft vine maples
approach_variants.notes: From the Gorge Creek Overlook parking area near 1,100 ft, cross the footbridge and start climbing essentially straight up the slope above; the bearing is unsubtle and the line is narrow. The first thousand feet is the slowest of the day — fallen timber stacked like pick-up-sticks, young trees and burnt charcoal from the fire that ran through here — and can take an hour on its own. Cliff bands come at about 2,400 ft and again at about 2,800 ft and are bypassed on the right. Above them a network of animal paths climbs a slight ridge feature through open timber, which is the sign you are past both. Fill up at Gorge Creek: there is no reliable water above the lower forest.
hazards: Dense blowdown and burnt deadfall in the lower forest; deviating even a short way off the line puts you in far worse brush
Two cliff bands below 3,000 ft
Avalanche-prone snow on the slopes around Point 5,872 in shoulder-season conditions
Wet, slime-coated slabs near the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding: The ladder of four markers, then a hard left under the slabs. From about 3,800 ft the route works left through vine maples to a partially snow-filled gully at roughly 4,000 ft; that gully leads to a tiny talus draw at about 4,500 ft, then to alpine snowfields near 4,800 ft, and the ground first looks promising at granite slabs around 4,850 ft, where the angle eases onto the southwest ridge crest. Take those four in order — vine maple, snow gully, tiny talus draw, granite slabs — and you are on the line. Stay left and north of Point 5,872 rather than committing to its slopes; parties have found avalanche-prone snow there and turned back, and the bump beyond it on the east ridge is a false summit, not Davis. At the top the buttress that looks steep and loose is reasonable Class 2-3 except for slime-coated slabs near the summit: the instruction is a hard leftward traverse, resisting the temptation to scramble the slabs. If you are on wet slab, you are off route.

bivy.name: Gorge Creek overlook, the trailhead you sleep at
bivy.notes: This is where the standard scramble starts, on Highway 20 between Newhalem and Diablo. You cross the creek on the bridge and go straight into steep forest with no trail of any kind. The peak is famous for the sheer drop off its far side, and the ground you climb reflects that: expect around ten miles and roughly seven and a half thousand feet of gain, with cliff bands to be turned in the timber around twenty-four hundred and twenty-eight hundred feet and a stretch of vine maple higher. Thirteen or fourteen hours car to car is a normal time for a fit party, and that is why so many sleep at the car rather than carry overnight gear up it. Being west of the seasonal highway gate, the pullout is reachable all year, but the route wants firm snow or dry ground rather than the rotten mix in between.
bivy.water: Gorge Creek itself, immediately below, and it is the last certain water for a long way up. Nothing is provided at the pullout.
bivy.permit: No permit and no fee to park or to sleep in a vehicle. A DAY climb from here needs no backcountry permit at all, which is the usual way this peak is done. The moment you sleep on the mountain you need a National Park Service backcountry permit for the Davis Peak cross-country zone.
bivy.capacity: A highway pullout and viewpoint parking area, not a campground. Parties routinely spend the night in a vehicle here to start at first light. There are no sites, no pitches, and nowhere to put a tent.

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, Newhalem
bivy.notes: About five minutes' drive west of the Gorge Creek overlook, this is the practical base for a party that wants a real campsite the night before rather than a night in the driver's seat. It is low, forested and close to the highway, with none of the character of the alpine above it, and that is fine for its purpose. It also stays open later in the year than the larger campgrounds nearby, which matters on a peak whose best conditions are often outside the busy season. The obvious closer option is gone: the small tent campground at Gorge Lake, right beside the creek in Diablo, has been shut for an extended period over debris-flow and flooding hazard on ground burned in an earlier fire, and should not be planned around without confirming it has reopened.
bivy.water: Potable water while the campground is serviced; the river is the fallback and needs treating. Availability drops off outside the main season.
bivy.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. No backcountry permit needed to sleep here. It has historically been the free, year-round, minimal-service option in the Newhalem cluster while the fee campgrounds close for winter — confirm the current fee and season, because the park has been adjusting both.
bivy.capacity: A modest road campground on the Skagit with a mix of standard sites and a couple of group sites, small enough that a busy summer weekend fills it.

bivy.name: Snowfield benches on the south side, around 4,800 feet
bivy.notes: The forest below is the whole difficulty of this mountain — steep, tangled and unrelenting, with the route picked out along animal paths and through weaknesses in the cliff bands. Getting up to this level and stopping turns a punishing single day into a manageable two, and this is the first ground on the route where a party can lie flat and see out. A partly snow-filled gully around four thousand feet is the usual way through the last of the trees onto these slopes; it is straightforward when it holds firm snow and considerably less pleasant when it is running wet or bare. Early summer is the moment for this camp, because the same snow that makes the gully work is what supplies the water.
bivy.water: Running snowmelt while there is snow, which is exactly what makes this level worth stopping at. Once the slopes bare out later in summer, water here becomes unreliable and the gully lower down is the last dependable source.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required for the Davis Peak cross-country zone: six people maximum in a party, and a maximum of three parties in the zone on any night. Walk-up only, collected in person at the Marblemount wilderness office rather than reserved in advance. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and not in meadow or within a hundred feet of water. No fires anywhere in the zone. Pack waste out where the ground will not take a cathole.
bivy.capacity: Open ground rather than sites. Where the timber finally releases into alpine snow and slabs there is room for a small party to lie down, and no established platform to aim for.

bivy.name: The 5,720 ft saddle south of the summit
bivy.notes: A little over half a mile south of the summit, this notch in the ridge is the highest sensible sleeping ground on the peak and the launching point for the last of the climbing. From here the standard finish takes the rock buttress on the south ridge at easy scrambling, a couple of grades of hands-on ground rather than anything technical. Parties have also tried the broad snow slopes of the east ridge from the saddle and been stopped by a step a few hundred feet under the top, so the south side is the line to plan for. Being a saddle it is exposed to whatever the weather is doing and there is nothing to shelter behind, which argues for using it on a settled forecast and otherwise sleeping lower. Note the other approach: the peak's steep north-east side is reached instead from the Stetattle Creek trail out of Diablo, leaving the path after a couple of miles and fording the creek — but that trail has been closed outright for falling dead trees on burned ground, so treat the Gorge Creek side as the only way in until it reopens.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and only while snow is present at the notch. Late in a dry summer there is nothing here and everything has to be carried up from the snowfields below.
bivy.permit: Same National Park Service backcountry permit and Davis Peak cross-country zone as the ground below: party of six maximum, three parties per night, walk-up from Marblemount, no fires, durable surfaces only.
bivy.capacity: Room for about two small tents on a snow ledge by the saddle. That is the whole capacity, and it is not a place to plan on sharing.

backups.fa: Wesley Grande and Jack Kendrick, 1947 (first ascent of the peak)
gear: light alpine rack to ~2 in (small-to-medium cams/nuts) for the mid-5th-class step and moat anchors
60m rope recommended for the descent's rappels (older 30m-rope beta is outdated for the standard multi-rappel line)

backups.overview: Mix-up Peak (7,440 ft) sits one mile south of Cascade Pass on the Skagit–Chelan county line and marks the northern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse. First climbed in 1947 by Wesley Grande and Jack Kendrick, its East Face is a compact, mostly solid-rock 'staircase' of class 3–4 scrambling with a short mid-5th-class step near the top, reached by a glacier/snowfield crossing from Cascade Pass. It's a popular objective (7-9 hours from the trailhead to the summit alone) for parties already in the Cascade Pass basin, but the approach's moat and rockfall-prone notches keep it a genuine alpine outing despite the modest elevation.
backups.beta: From Cascade Pass, contour south up Mixup Arm and across a roughly 6,000 ft bench to a small glacier/snowfield below Gunsight Notch; rope up to cross it. From the notch's south side, two roped pitches (a loose gully, then a short chimney/scramble) gain a shoulder below the main summit pyramid. From there, easy class 3-4 scrambling up the light-gray 'white staircase' leads to a short mid-5th-class step through a notch in the exposed summit ridge, then a short class 3-4 ridge walk to the true summit. Descend the same line via 5 rappels.
backups.turnaround: No official turnaround time is published, but given the 7-9 hour trailhead-to-summit estimate and the risk of downclimbing or rappelling loose rock after dark, most parties plan to be off the summit and back through Gunsight Notch by early-to-mid afternoon, especially when thunderstorms are in the forecast.
backups.rappels: ~5 rappels with a single 60 m rope, or 3 with two 60 m ropes; one lower rappel is overhanging
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.descent: Not a simple reverse of the ascent: most parties make several rappels (commonly cited as up to 5) back down through Gunsight Notch, including one overhanging double-rope rappel just below/north of the notch, then re-descend the glacier/snowfield and Mixup Arm to Cascade Pass. A 60m rope is recommended for the standard rappel line — the older single-30m-rope beta undersells what's needed. Move away from the fall line immediately after rappelling; rockfall knocked loose by the party above or below is a recognized hazard on this descent.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Cascade River Road, 23.1 mi from Marblemount; Northwest Forest Pass required, self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road (FR 15) to its end at the Cascade Pass Trailhead at about 3,600 ft, 23.1 miles from Marblemount. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, with a self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk; North Cascades backcountry permits should be reserved at least two days ahead if you plan to camp.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Trail junction with post marked for Stehekin; leave the maintained trail here and head south up open heather/talus toward the Ptarmigan Traverse.
waypoints.directions: Follow the well-graded, switchbacking Cascade Pass Trail 3.5 to 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft. There is no reliable water at the pass beyond seasonal snowmelt, so fill up at a creek crossing lower on the trail.

waypoints.name: Cache Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Traverse the lower Cache Glacier below Cache Col; rope up for crevasses, softening snow bridges by midday in summer.
waypoints.directions: From the pass do not continue on the maintained Stehekin trail. Pick up the climbers' path on the right, south side that bends south-southeast and makes a rising traverse across the heather and talus of Mixup Arm and Mix-up's east slopes at roughly the 6,000 ft contour, crossing a minor spur ridge and several steep snow gullies that hold snow well into summer. Early in the season those gullies have poor runout above a drop of some 400 ft, so an ice axe and comfort traversing firm snow matter here. The traverse ends at the toe of the Cache Glacier around 6,000 to 6,200 ft, where crevasses warrant a rope in early to mid season.

waypoints.name: Gunsight Notch
waypoints.note: Narrow gap in the ridge (portal used for Mix-up, Triplets and Cascade Peak); pass through and drop into the basin below Mix-up's east face - also the rappel exit on descent.
waypoints.directions: Ascend moderate glaciated and snow slopes toward the obvious notch system below and left of the summit, the so-called V-notch just north of Gunsight Notch, the main portal between Mix-up, the Triplets and Cascade Peak. Gain the notch by a short snow or scree gully; the technical crux for many parties is exiting the bergschrund or moat below it, which can reach mid-5th class on loose, dirty rock. Note that camping is prohibited at Cascade Pass and on Mixup Arm, so parties either do this as a long day or camp on past toward Kool-Aid Lake or Cache Col.

waypoints.name: East Face rock bands / gullies
waypoints.note: Ledge-and-gully system through broken rock bands leading to the summit block; loose rock common, watch for parties above.
waypoints.directions: From the south side of the notch work up Class 3-4 ramps on the east side to the light-gray feature climbers call the White Staircase, exposed but generally solid Class 3 with loose, dirty sections. It leads to a shoulder below the summit pyramid and on to a point roughly 100 ft below the top where the roped pitches begin. Rockfall, both natural and climber-triggered, is a real hazard through these gullies, so keep parties tight and helmets on well before roping up.

waypoints.name: Mix-up Peak Summit
waypoints.note: Low fifth-class summit moves gain the true summit; descend via several rappels back through Gunsight Notch.
waypoints.directions: The last hundred feet or so steepens into a short, sustained low- to mid-5th-class step on compact, occasionally dirty rock, protected with natural gear rather than bolts. It tops out on the exposed summit ridge a few yards from the true summit, leaving a short unroped scramble to the top before the rappel descent begins.

backups.detailed_rack: A light selection of cams and nuts up to 2 inches handles the brief fifth-class steps.
what_to_bring: glacier travel kit (harness, prusiks or mechanical ascender, slings)
optional 20m accessory cord + 1 picket for the Gunsight Notch moat in late season
pro_tips: Aim directly for the right-hand 'V-notch' (Gunsight Notch) rather than the left 'U-notch' to save time and avoid an unnecessary wrap-around
Carry a 60m rope for the descent — a single 30m rope, as sometimes suggested, understates what's needed for the standard multi-rappel line
A short 20m accessory line plus one picket can help fix a line across the Gunsight Notch moat when it's wide
Go midweek or after Labor Day for much better odds of a same-day walk-up wilderness permit at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center
watch_out: The moat/bergschrund at Gunsight Notch widens as the season progresses and can require an extra fixed line (~20m) and a picket to cross safely by late summer
Easy to mistake the left 'U-notch' for the correct right-hand 'V-notch' (Gunsight Notch), adding time and unnecessary exposure wrapping around
Rock quality is noticeably better on the true East Face than on the crumbly SE approach face — stay on-route
backups.pro_needs: Gear is used sparingly: a light rack (small-to-medium cams/nuts to ~2in) covers the short mid-5th-class step and any anchor-building at the moat/notch. Most of the route is unroped class 3-4 scrambling on solid rock.
backups.best_season: Late July through September — the Mixup Arm snowfield/glacier crossing and the Gunsight Notch moat are not reliably safe to cross until mid-to-late July most years (NPS won't reserve Cascade Pass-basin wilderness camps for trips starting before July 1 due to lingering snow); conditions generally hold through September before fall snow returns.
backups.approach: Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road (Forest Road 15), elevation ~3,600 ft. Follow the Cascade Pass Trail (a well-graded, switchbacking National Park trail, unnumbered but universally called the Cascade Pass Trail) 3.5-3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft of gain to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft) — a broad, scenic saddle with no reliable water beyond seasonal snowmelt, so top off at a creek crossing lower on the trail. From the pass, do not continue on the maintained Pacific Crest/Stehekin trail; instead pick up a climbers' path on the right (south) side that bends SSE and makes a rising traverse across the heather-and-talus flanks of Mixup Arm and Mixup Peak's east slopes at roughly the 6,000 ft contour. This traverse crosses a minor spur ridge and several steep snow gullies that hold snow well into summer — in early season these have poor runout above a roughly 400 ft drop, so an ice axe and comfort with a traverse on firm snow are important; a slip here has real consequences. Continue traversing to the toe of the Cache Glacier (~6,000-6,200 ft), then ascend moderate glaciated/snow slopes (watch for crevasses in early-mid season) aiming for the obvious notch system below and left of Mixup's summit — commonly called the 'V-notch' — just north of Gunsight Notch, the main portal between Mixup, the Triplets, and Cascade Peak. Gain the notch/saddle via a short snow or scree gully, then work up class 3-4 ramps on the east side to a feature climbers call the 'White Staircase' (exposed class 3), which leads to a point roughly 100 ft below the summit where the roped mid-5th-class pitches of the East Face/East Buttress begin. Camping is prohibited at Cascade Pass itself and on Mixup Arm, so parties either push the whole approach and climb as one very long car-to-car day (7-9 hours to the summit alone), or continue past the notch/Cache Col area to established sites at Kool-Aid Lake (~6,120 ft) or near Cache Col for a lower-effort summit day. Rockfall — both natural and climber-triggered — is a real hazard on the upper approach gullies and staircase; keep parties tight and helmets on well before roping up.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the final scramble pitches/downclimbing back to the top of the technical face (the uppermost section is a downclimb/scramble to the top of the East Face), then begin a rappel sequence rather than trying to downclimb the buttress itself — the rock is loose enough that down-climbing the route is not recommended. From a small ledge/anchor on the east side just below the summit, a 50 m rappel gets you down the steepest upper wall (rockfall-prone — the next rappeller should move off to the side immediately, not straight down, to avoid anyone above). Below that, parties generally find 2-3 more rappel stations working down toward the notch system: a single 60 m rappel to a belay/anchor stance, followed by an overhanging section that's typically rappelled on doubled rope (i.e., a full 60 m rope folded, giving ~28-30 m of rappel) down to just below (north side of) Gunsight Notch/the V-notch. Accounts are not fully consistent on the exact count — some describe essentially 3 key rappels down this line, others log 4, and one description notes '5 rappels will get you down... a 60 m rope is long enough' — the variance reflects rope length used and which anchors parties link together. Plan on 4-5 rappels with a single 60 m rope (or 2x 30 m/60 m doubled) to be safe, and treat 3 as an optimistic minimum if you're able to link stations with a full 60 m strand. Anchors are natural/fixed, not bolted: expect slung trees, horns, and boulders with aging webbing/cord — inspect every anchor before weighting it, back it up if it looks tired, and carry a knife and spare cord/webbing since parties have had to replace or rebuild anchors mid-descent. The first station below the staircase is reportedly in a tree at the top of the drop overlooking the V-notch. Once down to the notch, reverse the snow/scree gully and the traverse back across Mixup's east flank to Cascade Pass and out the trail to the trailhead; if you camped at Cache Col/Kool-Aid Lake, break camp there instead of continuing all the way to the car. Watch for rockfall from parties above throughout the descent, and be alert for a moated-out Cache Col in late season if that's part of your exit.
backups.bail: Retreat from the notch or moat is straightforward by reversing back down Mixup Arm to Cascade Pass. If partway up the face, prefer downclimbing over building an improvised rappel anchor — belay/rap stations off the established line are sparse and the rock is looser away from the standard route.

pitch_detail.notes: Above the White Staircase (exposed Class 3) the route gains a shoulder below the summit pyramid, then follows ramps and a short gully on the upper east side — sustained, exposed Class 4 on rock that is generally solid but has loose, dirty sections; many parties belay this pitch even though it is mostly scrambling terrain. Natural gear (horns, boulders, occasional slung block) protects it, matching the descent's reliance on natural anchors rather than bolts.

The last roughly 100 ft below the summit steepens into a short, sustained mid/low-5th-class step on compact rock (occasionally dirty) — the technical crux of the route, beginning about 100 ft below the top. It tops out onto the exposed summit ridge a few yards from the true summit, after which it's an unroped scramble to the top before starting the rappel descent back toward Gunsight/V-notch.
pitch_detail.anchor: Walk-off (no belay) — short scramble to the summit

itinerary.cal: North Cascades NP backcountry permits are required year-round (reserve at least 2 days ahead via recreation.gov); camping is not allowed at Cascade Pass or on Mixup Arm, so use the Cache Col/Kool-Aid Lake camp options instead.

days.note: Drive Cascade River Road to the Cascade Pass Trailhead (~3,600 ft) and hike the Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 mi to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft). Camping is not permitted at the pass or on Mixup Arm itself, so continue past the pass toward the Cache Col basin (~6,100-6,900 ft) — either the permitted shoulder site south of Cache Glacier or the no-permit Kool-Aid Lake site — and set up camp with a view toward Gunsight Notch.
days.title: Approach to high camp

days.note: An alpine start to cross the Mixup Arm glacier/snowfield while it's firm, a technical crux exiting the bergschrund/moat below Gunsight Notch, two pitches of 3rd-to-mid-5th-class rock to the 7,440 ft summit, then a multi-rappel descent (a double-rope rap plus two single-rope raps to the V notch, a one-at-a-time downclimb of a loose gully, and a short final rap back into the moat) before breaking camp and hiking all the way out to the trailhead.

climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate: heavy, wet snow accumulates through winter on the approach slopes, and the Mixup Arm snowfield/glacier crossing typically isn't reliably safe until mid-to-late July, with snow sometimes lingering on face ledges into August in a heavy year. Summers are generally stable under the Pacific high, but afternoon cumulus buildup and thunderstorms occur; check NWAC and the NPS backcountry conditions page before committing to the glacier crossing.

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass, Mixup Arm bench and the Cache Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade River Road runs about 22-23 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead at 3,600 ft. Follow the maintained Cascade Pass Trail 3.5-3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to the pass at roughly 5,400 ft. There is no reliable water at the pass beyond seasonal snowmelt, so fill at a creek crossing lower down.

At the pass, near the benches, turn right (south) onto the obvious climbers' path — do not continue on the maintained trail toward Stehekin. The path bends south-southeast and makes a rising traverse across heather and talus on the flanks of Mixup Arm and Mixup Peak's east slopes at roughly the 6,000 ft contour, crossing a minor spur ridge.

This traverse crosses steep snow gullies that hold snow well into summer. In early season the runout is bad — a slip has a drop of several hundred feet below it — so an ice axe and genuine comfort on firm snow traverses are the entry requirement, not optional extras.

Continue to the toe of the Cache Glacier at about 6,000-6,200 ft. The described landmark is a seasonal waterfall: walk past it, turn right, and ascend the lobe of the Cache.

Camping is prohibited at Cascade Pass and on Mixup Arm, so this is either a long car-to-car day of 7-9 hours to the summit, or you continue past the notch to established sites at Kool-Aid Lake (about 6,120 ft) or near Cache Col.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; access gets harder through August as the Cache Glacier recedes
hazards: Steep snow gullies on the traverse with a bad runout in early season
Wrong notch — U-notch on the left versus V-notch on the right
Bergschrunds flanking the snow tongue, ten to fifteen feet down to rock
Rockfall, natural and climber-triggered, on the upper gullies and staircase
Moat at the glacier-rock junction, worsening through the season and year on year
No camping permitted at Cascade Pass or on Mixup Arm
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There are two notches at the head of the Cache Glacier on Mixup's east side, and picking the wrong one is the standard mistake.

A U-shaped notch sits on the left and a V-shaped notch on the right. The East Face is accessed from the V-notch. It is common — and accepted — to go up through the U-notch on the left and wrap around the back side to reach the V, so being at the U is not a failure, but starting to climb from it is.

Gunsight Notch, the prominent notch west of Cache Col, is the portal that serves Mix-Up, the Triplets and Cascade Peak, and the snow tongue leading to it is short, about a hundred feet, but steep at roughly 50-65 degrees. Bergschrunds flank the tongue on either side, dropping ten to fifteen feet to a rock floor, and the ground between the snow and the rock is wet, tight and swept by rockfall.

From the south side of the notch the sequence is specific and is your confirmation: go west about 100 ft down a side gully, then ascend northwest up a wide, loose gully to a saddle. At that saddle the White Staircase begins — an easy, exposed class 3 staircase of pale grey rock on the right-hand side of the large summit pyramid. If you are looking at a grey staircase-like ramp on the right side of the pyramid, you are exactly where you should be.

The hardest and dirtiest climbing on the whole approach is the first fifty feet out of the moat where the glacier meets rock — perhaps mid-fifth on loose ground. That difficulty is itself a tell: if the entry felt trivial, check that you have actually crossed the moat at the right place.

Season matters for this specifically. As the Cache Glacier recedes, getting to the notch has been getting harder year on year, and by August the moat can be the deciding problem rather than the climbing.

climbing_route.label: Ramps on the east side above the notch
climbing_route.notes: From the notch/saddle below and left of the summit (the 'V-notch', just north of Gunsight Notch), gained via a short snow or scree gully, work up class 3-4 ramps on the east side. Rockfall — both natural and climber-triggered — is a real hazard on the upper approach gullies and staircase; keep parties tight and helmets on well before roping up.

climbing_route.label: The 'White Staircase'
climbing_route.notes: The ramps lead to a feature climbers call the 'White Staircase', exposed class 3, which leads to a point roughly 100 ft below the summit. Rockfall on the staircase is a real hazard.

climbing_route.label: Roped East Face/East Buttress pitches
climbing_route.notes: Roughly 100 ft below the summit the roped mid-5th-class pitches of the East Face/East Buttress begin.

bivy.name: Johannesburg Camp
bivy.notes: A walk-in camp a short, steep and often slick few minutes above the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the road — not a drive-up campground, you carry everything in. It is the practical staging point for the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir, Cascade Peak, and any pre-dawn start where you want to be at the road end the night before. If it is full, Marble Creek and Mineral Park down the Cascade River Road are the car campgrounds, at the cost of driving the rough section twice.
bivy.water: A creek runs beside the sites and normally holds water through the season, being fed by drainage off the north side of Johannesburg Mountain rather than by a single small snowfield.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required even though the camp is minutes from the car; Cascade River Road permits are issued in person at Marblemount, part reservable on Recreation.gov and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.capacity: Three small primitive sites, so it is easily filled by one or two parties.

backups.overview: Mount Price is the solitary high point of a ridge system between the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Dingford Creek in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, dwarfed by neighboring Big Snow Mountain but standing out as a distinct summit when viewed from other Alpine Lakes peaks. The north route follows the mountain's north ridge, reached via a long, mostly off-trail approach past Hester Lake — a quiet, rarely-climbed objective.
backups.beta: accounts describe three commonly used lines up Mount Price: this North Route (Dingford Creek/Goat Creek drainage), a route via Hester Lake on the northeast side, and a southeast-slope route. The North Route follows the Dingford Creek Trail about 2.1 miles (4-5 creek crossings), then leaves the trail near Goat Creek (~2,570 ft), crosses Dingford Creek, and climbs cross-country on a bearing of roughly 130°, staying below cliff bands on an ascending traverse to the saddle northwest of Little Hester Lake, then follows the ridge south to the 5,587-5,592 ft summit. It is class 2-3 routefinding terrain with a short section of moss-covered boulder scrambling to gain the saddle.
backups.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time before starting — the cross-country traverse below the cliff bands and the boulder moves to the saddle are far slower and more hazardous to navigate in the dark or if benighted; plan for a full day given the ~10 mile round trip and 4,100 ft of off-trail gain.

backups.detailed_rack: No fixed rock gear is needed for the standard line. Most parties carry an ice axe and, depending on season, light traction for the upper ridge snow; a rope and a few slings could be carried for the ridge's single exposed move by less experienced scramblers, though most parties climb it unroped.
pro_tips: Genuinely remote — the unmaintained Hester Lake Trail and long off-trail sections mean solitude is close to guaranteed
Some lingering snow into early summer eases the devil's club brush low on the route but adds avalanche exposure higher up
watch_out: cliff bands and brush around the Hester Lake shoreline
loose rock on the upper north ridge
creek crossings on Dingford Creek
backups.pro_needs: Minimal to none — an unroped scramble; the exposed section is short and usually downclimbed or spotted rather than protected.
backups.best_season: Late July through August offers the best balance of snow-free travel on the ridge/cliff-band section and manageable (though still present) brush. Earlier-season parties (June–early July) trade thicker devil's club for firmer lingering snow that can ease travel through the brushy sections and allow glissading on descent — but add avalanche and stream-crossing considerations.
backups.approach: Drive Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FR-56) from North Bend roughly 17-18 miles to the Dingford Creek / Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead. Hike Dingford Creek Trail about 3 miles, then follow the unmaintained Hester Lake Trail and off-trail terrain past Hester and Little Hester Lakes to reach the base of Mount Price's north ridge; a long day (roughly 15 miles round trip with 4,000+ ft gain) or overnight.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the north ridge and off-trail route back past Hester Lake to the Dingford Creek Trail and trailhead.
backups.bail: Retreat by reversing the ridge to the saddle and the traverse below the cliff bands; the crux on the way down is staying on the correct traverse line, so mark or GPS-track it on the way up before continuing above it.

pitch_detail.notes: ~4,400-5,100 ft: ascend the obvious talus slope directly or along its west side to the East-West ridge crest.
~5,100-5,587 ft: turn west and follow the steep, forested north side of the ridge to the summit; the route's single tricky move is on this section once snow is off.

itinerary.cal: Dingford Creek Rd (FR 5620) and the trail's creek crossings are best done after spring snowmelt/high runoff subsides, roughly July–October; snow can linger on the upper ridge into early summer.

days.note: A long single-day scramble: hike the boggy Hester Lake Trail into the basin below Little Hester Lake, traverse below the cliff bands to the tarn on the north side, gain the 4,680 ft saddle NW of Little Hester Lake, then scramble the south ridge to the summit. Reverse the entire route to descend, watching the clock since the trail's stream crossings and brush are unpleasant in the dark.

bivy.name: Hester Lake and Myrtle Lake basins
bivy.notes: This is the real base camp for Mount Price, and the only one. The Dingford Creek trail climbs steeply from the trailhead, passes the Myrtle Lake junction at a little over three miles, and reaches Hester Lake at around five and a half; beyond the junction the tread deteriorates noticeably and the crossings multiply. Price rises directly above Hester, and both the Hester Lake Route and the North Route stage out of this basin, so a party camping here is looking at their objective from the tent. Myrtle is the softer option if the day runs out early, but it puts you further from the peak. Snow lingers in these basins into June and the summit slopes hold it later, so July through early October is the window. With the road washout in place the whole trip is several miles longer each way, which pushes this from a fit party's long day firmly into an overnight.
bivy.water: Both lakes are reliable all season, and Dingford Creek runs the length of the approach. Filter or treat.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead: fill it in, drop the stub in the box, carry your copy. No parking pass is currently required at the trailhead. Group size is capped at twelve people. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the wilderness; both lakes sit just under that line so a fire is technically legal, but the ground is thin and the sites are heavily used, and stoves are the better answer. Seasonal fire bans override all of that and are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A few established, flat tent spots at Hester Lake, enough for two or three parties before it feels crowded. Myrtle Lake, at about 3,780 ft and a couple of miles nearer the road, has a smaller number of rougher sites.

bivy.name: Middle Fork Campground
bivy.notes: The only developed drive-in camping on the Middle Fork road, and the practical roadhead base for every peak in this zone. It sits at about road mile twelve, a few minutes below the Middle Fork trailhead, so a party sleeping here is already at the start of the Preacher Mountain approach and within a short drive of the Garfield pull-outs. The road to it is paved the whole way now, which is a recent change and makes this reachable in any car. Season is roughly mid-May to mid-September; outside those months the gate is shut and the valley has no legal developed option at all. Book ahead, because this is the closest forest campground to Seattle and summer weekends fill months in advance. For Mount Teneriffe parties it is the nearest legal camping of any kind, about twenty minutes' drive from that trailhead.
bivy.water: Potable water is provided from a solar-pumped system, but it has failed for stretches in recent seasons and been shut off mid-summer. Carry enough for the first night rather than counting on the tap. The river runs alongside the campground year-round and can be filtered.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, booked up to six months ahead through the federal reservation system or by phone; the adjacent day-use parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or a small daily fee. No wilderness permit applies at the campground itself. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine through late summer and one is in force at the time of writing, so confirm before planning a fire. A food storage order applies across the whole forest.
bivy.capacity: About 36 tent and trailer units plus a pair of group sites, no hookups, all reservable. Fourteen-day stay limit.

bivy.name: Middle Fork road pull-outs, Taylor River and Dingford Creek
bivy.notes: Worth reading before driving up with a plan to sleep in the back of the car, because the situation has changed and the change is not obvious on the ground. The lower valley is closed to dispersed camping, so the answer there is the campground or nothing. The Taylor River road is gated at the bridge at the end of the drivable road and its old roadbed is now the trail, so there is no driving in to a quieter spot. The upper road toward Dingford Creek is the one stretch still open to roadside camping, and it is cut by a washout at milepost 17.3 that closes vehicle access short of the Dingford Creek trailhead at 1,400 ft; the Forest Service's road-damage alert of June 30, 2026 lists it with no reopening date. That washout matters well beyond camping: with it in place the Mount Price approach and the Treen Peak path both gain several road miles on foot or bike each way, which turns two long days into overnight trips. Beyond the Dingford Creek trailhead the road has been gated to vehicles for years in any case. Road status in this valley changes year to year, so confirm the current state with the ranger district before committing; a party that discovers the washout at the barricade has lost the day.
bivy.water: The river and its side creeks are within a few minutes of the road the entire length of the valley and run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used corridor.
bivy.permit: This is the field that decides whether you can sleep here at all. A forest order closes dispersed camping along the road from the forest boundary up to the confluence of the Taylor and Middle Fork rivers, and along the Taylor River road out to the Snoqualmie Lake trailhead, including a quarter-mile strip on either side. That closure runs through the end of 2026 and covers essentially every pull-out parties used to use, including the ones nearest the Garfield approaches. Above the confluence, on the upper road toward Dingford Creek, roadside camping is not covered by the order. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or the interagency equivalent.
bivy.capacity: Informal gravel pull-outs only, a vehicle or two apiece, nothing signed, levelled or established.

backups.name: South Ridge
backups.fa: Unknown (first reported in 2006, with webbing already on the route)
hazards: Cannon hole gap
Moderate exposure
Weather window dependent
backups.overview: The classic route on South Peak following a scenic south-facing ridge. Features exposed granite climbing, clean in the opening corners but of marginal quality on the crest and around the arch, with memorable features including a notable gap called the 'cannon hole'.
backups.beta: Begin at one of two obvious dihedrals on the west side of the ridge south of the peak (accessible from Blue Lake). The first pitch climbs either of two clean corners to the ridge crest with chickenheads and good face features (5.7). The memorable traverse pitch crosses the gapping cannon hole (5.8), a feature which appeared sometime in the 1980s or 1990s. The final pitch is low 5th class scrambling to the summit block.
backups.turnaround: Given the multi-day, glacier-crossing approach and complete lack of nearby rescue infrastructure, this is not a route to push on a marginal forecast — plan to be off the summit and back across the glacier well before dark or before weather closes in.
backups.rappels: 2 — about 35 m north off the summit, then east onto the Blue Glacier
backups.comms: No documented cell coverage; parties describe this as one of the most remote climbing areas in the lower 48 — a satellite communicator or messenger is strongly advised.
backups.descent: Do not reverse the ridge. From the summit a rappel of roughly 35 m drops north off the top, and a second rappel takes you east onto the Blue Glacier, which drains the peak's east side. Expect a moat where rock meets ice — parties here have repeatedly found a deep gap at the base, and at least one rappel on this side hung free over it, so plan to land beyond the lip and carry enough cord to leave an anchor. Heading back toward the Chickamin Glacier and the Ptarmigan Traverse camps, cross the south ridge at the first col south of the South Peak; the second col is a common mistake, and one party describes losing time and backtracking after heading there.
obj_haz: glacier crevasses and creek crossings on approach

waypoints.name: Downey Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Corrected - previous waypoints incorrectly placed this route ~59 miles away at Amphitheater Mountain (Pasayten Wilderness), a research error. South Peak is actually part of the Gunsight Range, Glacier Peak Wilderness - same remote 2-day approach as Middle Peak (Downey/Bachelor Creek trail to Itswoot Ridge, Dome-Chickamin col, Chickamin Glacier).

waypoints.name: South Peak (Gunsight Range)
waypoints.note: A real, distinct summit — the southernmost of four named summits (Northeast/North/Middle/South) along one short ridge crest, reached last in a north-to-south traverse after Middle Peak. This coordinate is a disclosed geometric estimate ~0.2mi south of Middle Peak's position (48.30571,-120.99439) along the ridge, not a directly measured fix.

backups.detailed_rack: Alpine rack with emphasis on small and medium cams, stoppers, and slings. Good anchoring equipment for rappels.
what_to_bring: Water and food for multi-day approach
pro_tips: Start before sunrise to have full daylight for climbing and descent
The cannon hole feature is the crux; scout it carefully before committing
This is the best route on South Peak due to excellent granite quality
The traverse pitch across the cannon hole is exposed but well-protected
watch_out: The cannon hole traverse pitch is very exposed; be confident with your protection and footwork
Weather deterioration is rapid in afternoon; plan early starts
backups.pro_needs: This route has solid granite and good protection opportunities throughout. The cannon hole pitch may require placement at a specific angle to span the gap.
backups.best_season: Late July through August when the granite is dry and weather windows allow safe climbing.
backups.approach: The genuine standard approach is from the Downey Creek Trailhead (off Suiattle River Road) via the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse — a rugged, largely off-trail alpine route over Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake and Bachelor Creek involving glacier travel and significant bushwhacking. Climbers typically budget a full day (or two) of approach before reaching the base of South Peak's granite faces; this is an experienced-mountaineers-only objective, not a roadside crag.
backups.descent_text: Do not reverse the ridge. Rappel about 35 m north off the summit, then make a second rappel east onto the Blue Glacier; a moat usually separates rock from ice at the bottom. Carry two 60 m ropes — joined, they give rappels of up to a full 60 m, enough to reach past the lip of the moat — and cord to leave an anchor.
backups.bail: Retreat down the same rappel line used for descent (~35 m north, then east to the glacier); the lower, easier ground can likely be downclimbed by a competent alpine party in an emergency.

pitch_detail.notes: Start up either of the two clean corners on the west side of the ridge, south of the peak; they reach the crest in about half a pitch. From the crest, move right on chickenheads and face holds. Above the corner the face can be coated in black lichen, with poor protection, and a solid anchor on the choss of the crest is hard to find. Carry slings and small gear for it.

A short pitch across the Cannon Hole, a natural arch between two small towers that formed in a rockfall in the 1980s or 1990s. The crossing opens with an exposed lean from a knife edge onto the rock of the arch, then traverses over it. The rock around the arch looks unstable, so move gently.

It is given as low fifth class to the summit, but the line is not obvious: going both high and low tends to dead-end near a notch with old tat. One way through is a delicate, very exposed stem around a corner (graded 5.8–5.9) and a downclimb into the notch, then dirty low-fifth ground to the top. A follower on that step risks a pendulum, so consider rappelling it off the tat.

backups.itinerary: Multi-day trip from Stehekin (ferry up Lake Chelan, shuttle to High Bridge) or from Downey Creek in the west; plan 1-2 days of approach, a climbing day, and 1-2 days out.
