approach_variants.name: Downey Creek and the southern Ptarmigan corridor
approach_variants.notes: From the Downey Creek trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, work through the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse corridor over Itswoot Ridge and Cub Lake and up Bachelor Creek. Off-trail, brushy, and with glacier travel before you reach the peaks; a full day or two of approach is normal. Once in the basin, this route is reached from the lake side rather than from the glacier under the east faces.
approach_variants.season: July to September, once the approach is out of snow.
hazards: Long, committing off-trail approach with glacier travel
The cannonhole gap on the traverse pitch is exposed and the feature is relatively young rock
Weather-window dependent — this is a remote crest with no quick way off
Both start dihedrals look alike; picking the wrong one is harmless, picking the wrong face is not
approach_variants.baseFinding: Do not start under the summit — walk south along the foot of the ridge past it. The start is a pair of clean dihedrals side by side on the ridge's west flank, and the pair is the test: two obvious corners, either of which will take you to the crest, with nothing else of the kind nearby. Both give about a rope length of climbing on chickenheads and good face features once you step right out of the corner. The second confirmation is overhead and unmistakable: look along the ridge crest above you for the Cannonhole, a gap punched clean through the ridge, which the route traverses on its second pitch. If you cannot see a hole through the crest from where you are standing, you are not below this line. Negative markers: if you are under a single chimney tucked into the left side of a face directly beneath the summit, you have stopped short and are at the west face route; if you are on glacier ice with a moat between you and the rock, you have gone round to the east side entirely.

bivy.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
bivy.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
bivy.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
bivy.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
bivy.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road has been closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under a Forest Service order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028 unless rescinded sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. On top of that, the Forest Service's Miner's Fire order (06-05-26-17) closes the Downey Creek Trailhead, the Downey Creek Trail and the Bachelor Creek Trail from August 15 through December 31, 2026, unless rescinded sooner. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
bivy.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
bivy.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

backups.name: Northeast Ridge (1963 Route)
backups.season: Summer, when the low couloir approach still holds climbable snow
gear: small-medium alpine rock rack to 3 inches
ice axe and crampons for the couloir/glacier approach
hazards: Notorious rockfall hazard — the mountain is repeatedly called Beckey-era Cascades' 'most notorious' peak for danger, with loose rock cited across multiple trip reports and a documented near-miss rockfall incident on a 2020 descent
Frequent large avalanches/icefall from several hanging glaciers on the peak, including the Sill Glacier near this route
Steep (45–60°) snow sections on approach/descent with real fall consequence; one trip report calls the heather descent 'the most dangerous part of the trip'
Difficult, routefinding-intensive Doug's Direct descent through suspect rappel anchors and loose terrain, with a documented history of parties returning a day or two late
Cascade River crossing/ford required on approach
backups.overview: A more direct, all-rock alternative to the neighboring East Ridge and Northeast Buttress lines: climbs partway up the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir to a hanging glacier, then follows the leftmost rib to the summit, deliberately avoiding the brush that plagues the other routes.
backups.beta: Grade: 5.7+ YDS, Grade IV, 12 pitches, 4,000 feet. First ascent: 1963. Route: Climb partway up C-J couloir to hanging glacier on right; ascend leftmost rib to summit. Hazards: Objective danger from falling rock/ice, steep snow, exposed scrambling, avalanche potential. Equipment: Small-to-medium alpine rock rack (to 3 inches), 10+ runners, helmet. Best season: July-September. No bush climbing.
backups.turnaround: As with the mountain's other technical routes, set a firm turnaround time before committing above the couloir — the loose upper rib and long descent leave little margin if benighted.
backups.face: Northeast Face, above the hanging (Sill) glacier
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: Cell coverage in the Cascade Pass/Johannesburg cirque is unreliable; NPS advises never relying on a phone as a sole evacuation plan, though reception is occasionally possible from higher, more open terrain.
backups.descent: Not specifically documented for this route; climbers on Johannesburg's other technical lines typically descend via "Doug's Direct" (traversing beneath Cascade Peak/the Triplets and over Mixup Peak's north ridge to Cache Glacier) or by rappelling the East Ridge back to the Cascade-Johannesburg col.
obj_haz: Icefall/rockfall from the hanging (Sill) glacier during the approach traverse

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead (end of Cascade River Road)
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road to its end at the Cascade Pass trailhead, near 3,600 ft. The road is generally open late June through September, and this route's season is tied to it. This is one of the shortest approaches in the range: the serious ground starts around 3,500 ft, within an hour of the car, so there is no long walk to warm up on.

waypoints.name: Cascade River Crossing / Terminal Moraine
waypoints.note: Off-trail descent and ford of the infant Cascade River below the terminal moraine.

waypoints.name: Base of C-J Couloir
waypoints.note: Gain rock just before the Cascade-Johannesburg couloir narrows; the NE Ridge (1963) climbs the rib right of the couloir.

waypoints.name: Hanging Glacier Traverse
waypoints.note: Exposed rising traverse beneath Johannesburg's hanging glaciers; rockfall and icefall hazard.

timing.recommendedStart: Pre-dawn alpine start from a high bivy near the route's base, to be through the couloir/glacier crossing before daytime warming increases rock and icefall hazard

backups.detailed_rack: A small-to-medium alpine rock rack up to about 3 inches, 10+ runners/slings, plus ice axe and crampons for the couloir/glacier portion of the approach.
what_to_bring: light bivy gear as a contingency
pro_tips: The route stays on more solid, direct rock and avoids the brush of the neighboring Northeast Buttress lines by climbing partway up the C-J Couloir before cutting onto the leftmost rib.
watch_out: Like all of Johannesburg's northeast-side routes, the lower section shares exposure to icefall from the hanging glaciers above the couloir.
backups.pro_needs: Standard alpine rock rack to 3 inches with plenty of runners for the 12-pitch rib; supplement with snow/ice protection for the lower couloir approach.
backups.best_season: Late June through September, once the road is open and the lower couloir approach has consolidated snow.
backups.approach: East/Northeast from Cascade Pass trailhead; descend and cross Cascade River, then approach the northeast face via C-J couloir
backups.descent_text: From the summit, follow the East Ridge — downclimbing/rappelling loose, exposed 3rd/4th-class gendarme ledges (staying well below the crest) — to the Cascade-Johannesburg col. From the col, either rappel the C-J couloir or take the "Doug's Direct" line: traverse beneath the Triplets buttress, sidehill steep heather/meadow slopes, cross the north ridge of Mixup Peak, and descend to Cache Glacier, then follow the Cascade Pass trail back to the trailhead. This descent has taken other parties on Johannesburg's NE-aspect routes on the order of 4.5-9+ hours from the col.
backups.bail: Retreat from the upper rib is difficult on loose rock; parties are effectively committed once established above the C-J Couloir, generally continuing to the summit and descending via Doug's Direct or the East Ridge rappels.
backups.itinerary: Typically climbed over 2 days: Day 1 — approach from the Cascade Pass trailhead to a high bivy near the base of the Northeast Face/C-J couloir; Day 2 — climb the route to the summit, then descend via the East Ridge/C-J col and Doug's Direct back to the car (a long day; some parties add a 3rd day).

access.fees: No park entrance fee — North Cascades NP is fee-free. Summer-season backcountry permits (mid-May through early October) cost $10/person/night plus a $6 nonrefundable reservation fee; free outside that window.
access.notes: Wilderness permit required year-round for overnight stays in North Cascades National Park. Permits via Recreation.gov (60% reservation) or first-come-first-serve (40%). Cascade River Road (unpaved, 23 miles) opens late June/July. Free trailhead parking.
access.rules: No permit is required for a single-day climb; an overnight bivy or any backcountry camping requires a North Cascades NP wilderness/backcountry permit, reservable on Recreation.gov or obtained walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

FA audit: the on-file date '1963' is sourced only to a crowdsourced Mountain Project route page (submitted by a user in 2020), not a primary source (AAJ, Beckey guidebook, club journal). Other sources describe similar NE-side lines dated 1951 ('Northeast Rib') and 1957 ('NE Rib') — it's unclear whether this is a distinct route or a conflation/renaming of an earlier line. Treat '1963' as unverified rather than a confirmed historical FA date; no correction applied since no confident alternative was found either.

No climbers' names found for the Northeast Ridge (1963 Route) FA in any source checked (Mountain Project, Wikipedia, SummitPost, AAC Publications, CascadeClimbers). The mountain's overall FA (East Ridge/CJ Couloir, a different route) is well documented: July 26, 1938, by Calder Bressler, Bill Cox, Ray W. Clough, and Tom Myers (Wikipedia) — do not conflate with this route.

rappel_detail.pull: 60m. This first one is described either as a single rope-stretching rappel or split into two shorter ones to the block below.
rappel_detail.notes: Plan on a typical single-rope rappel. Begins the descent of the loose East Ridge crest toward C-J col.
hazards: parties who do not drop far enough below the crest end up committed to loose 4th and low-5th ground and have to climb back up to find the ledge with the cairns
anchors through this descent are mostly slings around large blocks, and some of the wrapped boulders are themselves suspect — check what the sling is attached to, not just the sling
rappel_detail.station: Not on the crest. Traverse the gendarmes on loose ledges roughly 40 to 75 ft below the ridge top, following occasional cairns, until the last two mini-summits come into view, then climb back onto the crest and look down the gully. The first anchors sit beside a small tower on the left side of that gully about 200 ft down, with a cairn on the tower in at least one season.

rappel_detail.pull: Carry spare cord and webbing — some stations are old tat and nothing else. A short rope leaves you between established anchors rather than at them.
hazards: stations are weathered tat and it is normal for the first person down to back one up with gear or add fresh sling
the rappel line is not the climbing line, so retrieving a stuck rope means climbing ground nobody in the party has been on
rappel_detail.station: A big block below the first anchors, where parties who split the opening rope-stretcher into two shorter raps end up.

rappel_detail.notes: A loose gully to climbers' right can be downclimbed instead of rappelled at various points.
hazards: the loose gully to climber's right of the rappels is the downclimbing alternative, and given how rotten the rock is, some parties consider downclimbing the safer of the two
rappel_detail.station: Continuing down the gully toward the heather benches. How many rappels this takes varies with rope length and how much of the loose gully a party is willing to downclimb, so the count between here and the benches is reported as two or three.

hazards: everything here is loose enough that a rappelling party showers the ground below it; take the gully one at a time rather than moving together
the heather feels less secure than the rock steps above it and is very hard to protect, which is the part of this descent accounts single out as genuinely dangerous rather than merely slow
rappel_detail.station: The last of the rappels into the heather benches. From here downclimb the heather to reach the next station.

hazards: aim straight at the col; lines that look more inviting trend away from it and cliff out, forcing a reversal late in the day
rappel_detail.station: A slightly hidden station below the heather benches — look for it before committing to more heather downclimbing, because it is easy to walk past.

rappel_detail.pull: 60m. Counts for the whole ridge vary widely with how much is downclimbed — anywhere from two rappels to eight is reported for the same line.
rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel of the sequence, reaching the Cascade-Johannesburg col.
rappel_detail.anchor: rap-sling anchor, East Ridge crest, above C-J col
hazards: the col sits at the head of the C-J couloir, which is a documented rock and icefall path — do not linger there and do not treat descending it as the easy way out
summit to col alone runs three to five hours, so parties routinely reach this last rappel at dusk with the long traverse out still ahead of them
rappel_detail.station: The final rappel, dropping below the heather benches onto moderately angled slabs directly above the Cascade-Johannesburg col.

backups.rappel_count_note: Not specifically documented for this route; the route's own beta says parties generally top out and descend via Doug's Direct (a non-rappel traverse) or by rappelling the East Ridge to the Cascade-Johannesburg (C-J) col, which is well documented for Johannesburg's other technical routes as roughly 7 single-rope rappels on rap-sling anchors down the ridge crest. Per-rappel lengths are not individually documented, so none are given here — plan on typical single-rope-length rappels; treat this as shared-route beta, not confirmed 1963-route-specific detail.

approach_variants.name: Straight off the road end: the C-J couloir to the hanging glacier, then the leftmost rib
approach_variants.notes:
This is one of the shortest approaches in the range and one of the least forgiving. From the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of Cascade River Road near 3,600 ft, walk a short way back down the road, descend a dirt embankment, ford or cross the infant Cascade River, and cross the terminal moraine and snowfield. Serious ground starts around 3,500 ft — you are on the route within an hour of the car.

Climb partway up the Cascade-Johannesburg couloir to the hanging glacier on the right, then take the leftmost rib to the summit. Twelve pitches, about 4,000 ft.

The descent is a separate expedition: the East Ridge's loose 3rd and 4th class gendarme ledges to the Cascade-Johannesburg col, then either the couloir or 'Doug's Direct' — beneath the Triplets buttress, sidehilling steep heather, across Mixup Peak's north ridge and down to the Cache Glacier. Parties have taken four and a half to nine hours from the col.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September, once the road is open and the lower couloir approach holds consolidated snow
hazards: Hanging glaciers above the route — the Sill Glacier among them — that release ice and rock; parties describe rocks and ice bouncing for three or four seconds at a time
The mountain's standing reputation for rockfall, with loose rock reported across trip reports and a documented near-miss on a 2020 descent
Steep 45-60 degree snow on approach and descent with real fall consequence — one party found the heather descent the most dangerous part of the trip
A Cascade River ford at the very start, which rises through the day
A routefinding-intensive descent with suspect rappel anchors, and a history of parties returning a day or two late
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The test for this route is whether you are touching vegetation, and it is the cleanest discriminator on the whole face. This side of Johannesburg carries at least five named lines within a few hundred metres of each other, and most of them start with hundreds of feet of vertical bushwhacking — alder, turf, tree roots, tunnelling through near-vertical pines. This route does not. Its own published description ends with the words no bush climbing. If you are pulling on trees or heather to make upward progress, you are on the northeast rib or the northeast buttress, not on this.

So the sequence is: stay in the couloir. Do not break out onto rock low down. Climb the Cascade-Johannesburg couloir until a hanging glacier appears on your right — that glacier is the landmark, and it is what you leave the couloir for. The Northeast Rib lines leave the couloir far lower, before it narrows.

From the hanging glacier, take the leftmost rib. That is the whole route-finding instruction and the word that matters is leftmost. Several rib features present themselves at that shelf; the correct one is the far left of them.

Orient yourself on the face as a whole before you start, because it is crowded: running west to east across it the order is the Northeast Rib lines, then a route in a vertical cleft with a waterfall, then the Northeast Buttress. The Cascade-Johannesburg couloir is the broad snow line that separates Johannesburg from Cascade Peak, and this route uses it as a stairway rather than climbing it to the col.

And know what the couloir itself is: it is the original 1938 line and the most popular one, finishing at the col rather than on any rib. If you are still in the snow at the top, you never left for the rib.

bivy.name: Johannesburg Camp
bivy.notes: A walk-in camp a short, steep and often slick few minutes above the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the road — not a drive-up campground, you carry everything in. It is the practical staging point for the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir, Cascade Peak, and any pre-dawn start where you want to be at the road end the night before. If it is full, Marble Creek and Mineral Park down the Cascade River Road are the car campgrounds, at the cost of driving the rough section twice.
bivy.water: A creek runs beside the sites and normally holds water through the season, being fed by drainage off the north side of Johannesburg Mountain rather than by a single small snowfield.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required even though the camp is minutes from the car; Cascade River Road permits are issued in person at Marblemount, part reservable on Recreation.gov and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.capacity: Three small primitive sites, so it is easily filled by one or two parties.

backups.overview: A short, easy-to-miss V0+ boulder problem on a flat-topped erratic beside the White Chuck Glacier basin, climbed almost in passing by parties on Glacier Peak's standard south-side approach.

The boulder stands west of what is left of the White Chuck Glacier, in view of the path, and is easy to recognise by its flat top; there is room for a single tent at its foot.

Land on pads, spot as usual for the topout, and watch footing on any wet rock or duff on the way down.
